topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Integers, factors and exact arithmetic

sections.heading: Structure before calculation
sections.body: An integer is a whole number, including zero and negative values. A prime has exactly two positive factors. Expressing a number as a product of primes exposes its structure: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. For a highest common factor, keep the smallest powers shared by both numbers. For a lowest common multiple, keep the largest powers appearing in either number.

sections.heading: Fractions and signs
sections.body: A fraction represents division. Use a common denominator to add or subtract; multiply numerators and denominators separately to multiply. Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal. Cancel common factors before multiplying to keep arithmetic manageable. A negative multiplied or divided by a negative gives a positive result; this sign rule does not replace the rules for addition.

sections.heading: Accuracy and sensible answers
sections.body: Use place value when rounding. Decimal places count digits after the decimal point; significant figures start at the first non-zero digit. Keep exact fractions during intermediate work and round at the end. Estimate before calculating so that a misplaced decimal point becomes obvious. Recurring decimals can be turned into fractions by multiplying to align the repeated blocks, then subtracting.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A prime-factor decomposition provides a useful check on both factor methods: HCF × LCM equals the product of the two positive starting integers. In a recurring-decimal conversion, choose powers of ten so the recurring blocks line up. If x = 0.272727…, then 100x − x = 27, giving x = 27/99 = 3/11. For a mixed recurring decimal, align the repeating section rather than subtracting digits that do not match. An exact answer keeps the fraction; a rounded decimal should carry the requested accuracy.

topics.tip: HCF cannot exceed either starting number. LCM must be divisible by both.

worked.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 90.
steps: The common factors with smallest powers give HCF = 2 × 3² = 18.
The largest powers give LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Powers, roots, standard form and surds

sections.heading: Indices describe repeated multiplication
sections.body: For the same non-zero base, multiply powers by adding indices and divide by subtracting them. Raising a power to a power multiplies the indices. A zero power is 1; a negative power means a reciprocal. A fractional power combines a root with a power: x^(2/3) is the cube root of x, squared, where the real expression is defined.

sections.heading: Scale without a long string of zeros
sections.body: Standard form is a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. Multiply the coefficients and the powers of ten separately, then renormalise. For addition, first express both values using the same power of ten. Your calculator display may use E to mean ×10 to a power, rather than the mathematical constant e.

sections.heading: Higher: keep irrational values exact
sections.body: Simplify a surd by extracting square factors: √72 = 6√2. Like surds combine as like algebraic terms; unlike surds usually do not. Rationalising a denominator changes the form without changing the value. For a two-term denominator, multiply by its conjugate so the denominator becomes a difference of squares. Keep an exact answer when the question requests one.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Index laws apply to multiplication of equal bases, not addition: 2³ + 2² is 12, not 2⁵. To rationalise 1/(√5 + 2), multiply by √5 − 2 on the top and bottom. The denominator becomes 5 − 4 = 1. When using fractional indices, check real-number restrictions before taking an even root. Standard form is useful for estimating as well as computing: a result with coefficient 0.6 must be rewritten as 6 × 10⁻¹ times the remaining power of ten.

topics.tip: √(a + b) is not generally √a + √b.
topics.formula: aᵐ × aⁿ = a^(m+n); (aᵐ)ⁿ = a^(mn)

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Ratio, percentages, bounds and variation

sections.heading: Choose the correct whole
sections.body: Ratios compare quantities in matching units. Divide a total by the sum of the ratio parts, then multiply by each share. Percentage change compares the change with the original amount. Growth uses a multiplier above 1 and depreciation a multiplier below 1. Reverse percentage problems start from the final amount, so divide by the multiplier.

sections.heading: Repeated change and proportional models
sections.body: Compound growth applies the multiplier repeatedly: P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. Direct proportion has the form y = kx, or a stated power of x; inverse proportion has the form y = k/x. Find k using a known pair before predicting a new value. Do not assume proportionality just because both quantities increase.

sections.heading: Bounds express what rounding hides
sections.body: A length rounded to the nearest centimetre has a half-centimetre interval on each side. The lower endpoint is included; the upper is excluded under the usual school convention. For a maximum quotient of positive measurements, use the largest numerator and smallest denominator. A degree-of-accuracy answer must be justified by agreement between the calculated bounds.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a measurement recorded as 8.2 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm, the underlying interval is 8.15 ≤ length < 8.25. A compound calculation must use the most extreme combination that actually maximises or minimises the result. In an inverse-square relationship, doubling the input divides the output by four. Translate words such as proportional to the square into y = kx² before substituting. Ratios can also describe rates, but quantities with different dimensions should keep their units, for example kilometres per hour.

topics.tip: Equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel.
topics.formula: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100

worked.question: A £240 bicycle is reduced by 15%, then the sale price rises by 10%. Find the final price.
steps: After the reduction: 240 × 0.85 = £204.
After the increase: 204 × 1.10 = £224.40.
The overall multiplier is 0.935, so the net change is a 6.5% decrease.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Algebraic manipulation and linear equations

sections.heading: An expression is not an equation
sections.body: Collect terms only when their variable parts match. Expand a bracket by multiplying every term inside it. Factorising reverses expansion: remove the highest common factor first. An identity is true for every allowed variable value; an equation normally restricts the possible values. Substitution into a formula must preserve brackets, especially around negative values.

sections.heading: Keep both sides balanced
sections.body: Solve linear equations by applying the same operation to each side. Clear fractions using a common multiple of the denominators, keeping every term. Rearranging a formula follows the same logic, although the result may remain symbolic. If the subject appears twice, collect its terms and factorise it before dividing.

sections.heading: Inequalities and simultaneous constraints
sections.body: Inequalities describe ranges, shown on a number line or coordinate region. Reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Simultaneous linear equations require both equations to hold: eliminate one variable using suitable multiples, or substitute one equation into the other. Check the resulting pair in both original equations.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Rearranging a formula can involve a variable on both sides. From y = ax/(x + b), multiply to get yx + yb = ax, collect x terms and factorise: yb = x(a − y). Thus x = yb/(a − y), provided the original expression and the final denominator are defined. For inequality regions, draw each boundary and test a point not on it. A dashed boundary usually excludes the line, while a solid boundary includes equality. State integer solutions separately when the variable is restricted to integers.

topics.tip: When clearing fractions, multiply every term, not just the fractional terms.

worked.question: Solve 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1.
steps: Add the equations to eliminate y: 3x = 12.
Therefore x = 4.
Substitute into x − y = 1: 4 − y = 1, so y = 3.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Quadratics, algebraic fractions and proof

sections.heading: Three routes to a quadratic solution
sections.body: Write ax² + bx + c = 0 before factorising. The zero-product rule then sets each factor equal to zero. Completing the square exposes the turning point and is useful for graph interpretation. The quadratic formula works when a is non-zero; the discriminant b² − 4ac distinguishes two real roots, one repeated real root or no real roots.

sections.heading: Higher: fractions and non-linear systems
sections.body: Factorise numerator and denominator before cancelling common factors in algebraic fractions. You cannot cancel separate added terms. Record excluded denominator values from the original expression. For a linear-quadratic simultaneous system, substitute the linear expression into the quadratic, solve the resulting equation and calculate a corresponding coordinate for each valid root.

sections.heading: Reasoning with general forms
sections.body: A proof must establish a claim for all permitted values, not a few numerical examples. Write an even integer as 2n and an odd integer as 2n + 1. Use algebra to expose the required property. For inequalities involving products, use the roots as boundaries and check the sign in each interval instead of assuming the solution lies between the roots.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Completing the square rewrites x² + 6x + 5 as (x + 3)² − 4, exposing a minimum at (−3, −4). For algebraic fractions, record excluded values before cancelling: (x² − 9)/(x − 3) simplifies to x + 3 only for x ≠ 3. A proof by contradiction starts from an assumption and reaches an impossibility; a counterexample disproves a universal claim with one valid failure. Numerical examples can suggest a pattern, but they cannot establish that it always holds.

topics.tip: A quadratic can have two solutions; include both unless context excludes one.

steps: Find factors with product −14 and sum −5: −7 and 2.

The two solutions are x = 7 and x = −2.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Sequences and function notation

sections.heading: From a pattern to a rule
sections.body: For an arithmetic sequence, consecutive terms differ by a constant. Its nth term is a + (n − 1)d. For a geometric sequence, consecutive terms have a constant ratio, giving ar^(n−1). A quadratic sequence has constant second differences; half that second difference is the coefficient of n². Subtract that quadratic part to identify the remaining linear expression.

sections.heading: A function maps an input to an output
sections.body: The notation f(x) names the rule, not multiplication of f by x. Substituting an expression means replacing every x with that entire expression in brackets. Composite functions apply the inside function first. An inverse undoes a function on a suitable domain: exchange input and output and rearrange, checking whether a restriction is needed for a unique inverse.

sections.heading: Higher: iteration and transformations
sections.body: An iterative rule repeatedly uses the previous estimate to produce the next. State the starting value and show the sequence of estimates to the requested accuracy. On graphs, f(x) + a shifts vertically, f(x − a) shifts right, af(x) scales vertically and f(ax) scales horizontally by reciprocal factor. Track coordinates rather than memorising a vague movement.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a quadratic sequence with terms 3, 8, 15, 24, the first differences are 5, 7, 9 and the second differences are 2. Start with n², then subtract its values from the terms to obtain 2, 4, 6, 8; the nth term is n² + 2n. For an inverse, the permitted domain matters: squaring loses the sign of an input, so x² has no unique inverse on all real numbers. A restricted non-negative domain permits the inverse square-root function.

topics.tip: f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) usually give different results.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Graphs, gradients and calculus

sections.heading: Read the relationship, not only the picture
sections.body: For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. Parallel straight lines have equal gradients; perpendicular non-vertical gradients have product −1. Use two points to calculate change in y divided by change in x. Plotting tables should include negative and zero inputs when appropriate, so the important shape is not missed.

sections.heading: Curves and real-life graphs
sections.body: Recognise quadratic, cubic, reciprocal and exponential shapes. Intersections represent simultaneous solutions. The gradient of a distance-time graph is speed; the gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration. Area under a velocity-time graph is displacement, so a region below the time axis contributes negatively. Use a tangent to estimate an instantaneous gradient.

sections.heading: Higher: differentiate polynomial terms
sections.body: Differentiation gives a gradient function. For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = anx^(n−1) for the polynomial terms studied here; constants differentiate to zero. Set the derivative equal to zero to find stationary points, then examine surrounding gradients or the curve. For a tangent at a point, calculate its gradient and substitute the point into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A tangent calculation requires both a point and a gradient. For y = x³ at x = 2, the derivative 3x² gives gradient 12 and the point is (2, 8), so the tangent is y − 8 = 12(x − 2). For an optimisation problem, define a variable, build a formula for the quantity to maximise or minimise, then differentiate. Check that the stationary point lies in the physical domain and that its type matches the question. Endpoints can also matter when a domain is bounded.

topics.tip: A zero gradient identifies a stationary point, not automatically a maximum.

worked.question: For y = x² − 4x + 1, find the stationary point.

Set the gradient to zero: 2x − 4 = 0, so x = 2.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Angles, constructions and circle reasoning

sections.heading: Build an angle argument
sections.body: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point to 360°, and in a triangle to 180°. Parallel lines create corresponding and alternate equal angles; co-interior angles sum to 180°. Name the reason for each step in a geometry proof. An n-sided polygon has interior-angle sum (n − 2) × 180°.

sections.heading: Circle theorems connect points
sections.body: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90°. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at contact, and tangents from an external point have equal lengths. The alternate segment theorem links a tangent-chord angle to the opposite arc angle.

sections.heading: Loci and accurate constructions
sections.body: A perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points. An angle bisector is equidistant from two intersecting lines. Keep compass arcs visible when a construction is required. Bearings are measured clockwise from north using three figures. Distinguish a diagram that supplies measurements from a sketch that is explicitly not drawn to scale.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A geometric proof should identify the exact points used by a theorem. If two angles stand on the same chord from the same segment, they are equal; angles on opposite segments can instead be supplementary. The sum of exterior angles of a convex polygon, taken one at each vertex in a consistent direction, is 360°. In a regular polygon each exterior angle is 360°/n. A locus diagram may require the intersection of several regions, so shade only points meeting every condition.

topics.tip: Circle theorems require points on the relevant circle and the correct arc.

steps: Use the centre-circumference relationship.

The required angle is 62°.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Mensuration, similarity and trigonometry

sections.heading: Measure in the correct dimension
sections.body: Area is two-dimensional; volume is three-dimensional. Convert lengths before applying formulae. A prism has constant cross-section, so volume is cross-sectional area × length. A pyramid or cone has volume one third of base area × perpendicular height. Arc length and sector area are the corresponding fraction of a full circumference or circle.

sections.heading: Similarity scales different quantities differently
sections.body: Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths. If the length scale factor is k, the area factor is k² and volume factor k³. Match corresponding sides before using the ratio. Congruent shapes are identical in size and shape, whereas similar shapes may be different sizes.

sections.heading: Choose a triangle method deliberately
sections.body: Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA apply to right-angled triangles. For other triangles, the sine rule relates opposite angle-side pairs and the cosine rule relates three sides or two sides with the included angle. The formula ½ab sin C gives the area using two sides and their included angle. Draw a clear diagram for three-dimensional problems and identify the right-angled triangle you actually use.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a non-right-angled triangle, pair each side with its opposite angle before applying the sine rule. When two sides and an included angle are known, the cosine rule finds the third side. Surface area must account for which faces are actually exposed; a joined solid may hide surfaces. For a frustum, subtract the smaller similar solid from the larger and use the linear scale factor to find missing dimensions. Retain exact multiples of π until a decimal answer is requested.

topics.tip: Use perpendicular height for area and volume; a sloping edge is usually different.
topics.formula: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; area = ½ab sin C

steps: The length scale factor is 10/4 = 2.5.

The larger volume is 32 × 15.625 = 500 cm³.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Vectors and transformation geometry

sections.heading: Describe the entire transformation
sections.body: A translation needs a column vector. A reflection needs a mirror line. A rotation needs a centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs a centre and scale factor; a negative factor places the image on the opposite side of the centre. Trace corresponding points to check your description. A transformation description should identify a single operation unless a combination is requested.

sections.heading: Vectors carry direction and magnitude
sections.body: Treat a vector as a displacement. Reversing its direction changes its sign. Adding vectors follows a connected route; subtracting position vectors gives the displacement between the two positions. Multiplying by a scalar changes magnitude and may reverse direction. Equal vectors need not start at the same point.

sections.heading: Higher: prove a geometric relationship
sections.body: Two non-zero vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other. To prove points are collinear, also show the relevant vectors share a point. Express a midpoint by averaging endpoint position vectors. For ratio division, use a consistent route from a known point and scale the entire displacement vector. Present each vector equality with its start and end points.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A vector proof can separate direction from position. Showing AB = 2CD establishes parallel directions with a 2:1 magnitude ratio, but says nothing about whether those segments lie on the same line. To divide AB internally in the ratio 2:3, start at A and travel 2/5 of the vector from A to B. For enlargements with a negative scale factor, image points lie on the opposite side of the centre. The magnitude of the factor sets their distance ratio.

topics.tip: Parallel vectors alone do not prove three points are collinear.

worked.question: Position vectors of A and B are a and b. Find the position vector of the midpoint M.
steps: The displacement from A to B is b − a.
Move halfway along it from A: a + ½(b − a).
Simplifying gives OM = ½(a + b).

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Data, distributions and statistical diagrams

sections.heading: A statistic answers a particular question
sections.body: The mean uses every value but is sensitive to extreme values. The median is the central ordered value. The mode is the most common value and may not be unique. The range describes total spread; the interquartile range describes the middle half. Compare both a measure of centre and a measure of spread when comparing distributions.

sections.heading: Grouped data and unequal intervals
sections.body: A mean estimated from grouped data uses class midpoints, multiplies each by its frequency, then divides by total frequency. It is an estimate because the individual values are unknown. For histograms, frequency is represented by area, not height: frequency density equals frequency divided by class width. Keep continuous class boundaries consistent.

sections.heading: Interpret relationships cautiously
sections.body: A scatter graph may suggest positive, negative or no correlation. A line of best fit supports interpolation within the observed range; extrapolation is less secure. Correlation alone does not establish cause. Cumulative frequency curves estimate medians and quartiles. A probability sample should reduce selection bias; explain how the sample represents the population rather than merely calling it random.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A grouped-data median is estimated from cumulative frequency at half the total frequency. The lower and upper quartiles correspond to one quarter and three quarters of the total. A box plot communicates these summaries but not the individual data values. In stratified sampling, allocate sample sizes in proportion to category sizes, then select appropriately within each category. A sample can be large yet biased if the selection excludes important parts of the population. Explain both the selection method and the population it represents.

topics.tip: For a histogram, compare bar areas when you need frequencies.
topics.formula: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width

worked.question: A histogram class 10–20 has frequency 30. A class 20–40 has frequency 40. Find both frequency densities.
steps: The first class width is 10 and its density is 30/10 = 3.
The second class width is 20 and its density is 40/20 = 2.
The first bar is taller even though its class has fewer observations.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Probability, sets and conditional events

sections.heading: List the sample space accurately
sections.body: Probabilities range from 0 to 1. Exhaustive mutually exclusive outcomes have probabilities summing to 1. The complement rule gives P(not A) = 1 − P(A). A sample-space diagram is useful only when its elementary outcomes are equally likely, or when each outcome is weighted correctly.

sections.heading: Trees and overlapping events
sections.body: Multiply probabilities along a complete tree path and add paths corresponding to the desired event. With no replacement, update both the category count and total before the second selection. For overlapping events, subtract the intersection when adding probabilities: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Venn diagrams help separate the regions.

sections.heading: Higher: conditions change the reference group
sections.body: Conditional probability restricts the denominator to outcomes satisfying the condition. P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B), when P(B) is non-zero. Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A)P(B); mutually exclusive events have no shared outcomes. These descriptions are not interchangeable. A tree can still describe dependent events, provided each branch probability uses the appropriate condition.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A condition restricts the sample space. If 12 pupils study both art and music and 20 study music, the probability of art given music is 12/20, not 12 divided by the whole school. In a Venn diagram, place the intersection first, then fill exclusive regions and finally the outside. For at least one success, calculating one minus no successes can be simpler than listing every successful path. State independence only when the process or the data supports it.

topics.tip: Without replacement normally means the draws are dependent.
topics.formula: P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B)

steps: The probability of red first is 3/5.
After a red draw, there are 2 red counters among 4 remaining, so the next probability is 2/4.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Life processes, groups and pathogens

sections.heading: What living systems do
sections.body: Living organisms carry out nutrition, respiration, excretion, response to surroundings, movement, growth and reproduction. A single organism need not reproduce during its lifetime to be alive. Cellular organisation connects molecules to cells, tissues, organs and organ systems. These levels describe increasing coordination, not simply increasing physical size.

sections.heading: Recognising the major groups
sections.body: Animals are multicellular, lack cell walls and obtain organic nutrients by feeding. Plants contain chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells and have cellulose cell walls. Fungi have chitin cell walls and feed by extracellular digestion followed by absorption. Protoctists are diverse eukaryotes, many of them single-celled. Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is not enclosed within a nucleus.

sections.heading: Pathogens are not a separate kingdom
sections.body: A pathogen causes disease. Some bacteria produce toxins or damage cells, but many bacteria are harmless or useful. Viruses are much smaller than cells and reproduce only inside host cells. A virus consists of genetic material inside a protein coat; it has no independent cellular metabolism. Antibiotics act on suitable bacterial targets and do not treat viral infections.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The distinction between eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisation concerns the nucleus and internal cell organisation, not simply cell size. A fungus can digest food outside its cells by secreting enzymes and then absorbing soluble products; this differs from ingesting solid food. A virus uses host-cell machinery to reproduce, so it is not described as a small bacterium. When comparing groups, choose corresponding features such as cell walls, genetic material, chloroplasts and nutritional method. A statement about a particular organism should not be applied automatically to every member of its group.

topics.tip: Do not describe every microorganism as harmful.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Cells, enzymes and membrane transport

sections.heading: Cell structures explain cell functions
sections.body: The nucleus contains genetic material; ribosomes synthesise proteins; mitochondria support aerobic respiration. Plant cells additionally have a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole, with chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells. Cell differentiation produces specialised structures. Stem cells can divide and differentiate; their use requires consideration of therapeutic benefits, tumour risk and ethical questions.

sections.heading: Enzymes work through a specific active site
sections.body: An enzyme is a biological catalyst. Substrates bind at an active site and products are released, leaving the enzyme available again. Heating initially increases collision frequency, but sufficiently high temperatures alter the active site and denature the enzyme. Extreme pH can do the same. Cooling normally slows activity rather than denaturing the protein.

sections.heading: Three different transport mechanisms
sections.body: Diffusion is net particle movement down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential. Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration. Large surface area, a thin barrier and a maintained concentration difference favour rapid exchange; cells with high active-transport demand often contain many mitochondria.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A small cell has a large surface-area-to-volume ratio compared with a larger geometrically similar cell. As cell dimensions increase, surface area grows with the square of length while volume grows with the cube. This can make exchange too slow relative to demand, helping explain specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. In an osmosis experiment, calculate percentage mass change to compare differently sized samples fairly. Keep solution concentration, temperature, sample preparation and duration controlled. A zero mass change indicates no net water movement under those conditions, not that water molecules have stopped crossing the membrane.

topics.tip: Osmosis concerns water; a definition about unspecified particles describes diffusion.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Nutrition and photosynthesis

sections.heading: Plants build organic molecules
sections.body: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, transferring light energy into chemical energy. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Glucose can fuel respiration, form cellulose, be stored as starch, or combine with mineral-derived nitrogen to make amino acids. Light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature may limit the rate; a plateau means another factor has become limiting.

sections.heading: Digestion turns food into absorbable molecules
sections.body: A balanced diet supplies carbohydrate, protein, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in appropriate proportions. Amylase breaks starch into sugars, proteases produce amino acids and lipases produce fatty acids and glycerol. Bile emulsifies fats and helps neutralise stomach acid. Villi provide a large thin exchange surface and a blood supply that maintains gradients; lacteals transport products of lipid absorption.

sections.heading: Practical evidence and controls
sections.body: For starch testing, decolourise a leaf using ethanol in a hot-water bath, rinse it, then add iodine. Blue-black indicates starch. Use a destarched plant and suitable light or carbon-dioxide controls to investigate requirements. For food tests, use iodine for starch, heated Benedict’s reagent for reducing sugar, Biuret reagent for protein and an ethanol emulsion test for lipids. Observe laboratory safety, particularly with flammable ethanol.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A leaf’s broad surface intercepts light, while its thin structure gives gases a short diffusion route. Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts and air spaces connect mesophyll surfaces to stomata. Magnesium is required for chlorophyll and nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids. In digestive questions, distinguish digestion, absorption and assimilation: digestion breaks large food molecules down, absorption moves soluble products into circulation, and assimilation incorporates or uses them in cells. Bile is not an enzyme; emulsification increases the area available for lipase without chemically hydrolysing lipid molecules.

topics.tip: Plants respire all the time; photosynthesis requires suitable light.
topics.formula: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Respiration, gas exchange and transport

sections.heading: Respiration releases usable energy
sections.body: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy for cellular processes. Anaerobic respiration in human muscle produces lactate and releases less energy per glucose. In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Breathing moves air; respiration is a cellular chemical process. Do not use the terms interchangeably.

sections.heading: Exchange surfaces maintain diffusion
sections.body: Alveoli provide a large moist surface, very thin walls and a dense capillary supply. Ventilation and blood flow maintain oxygen and carbon-dioxide gradients. In leaves, stomata open into air spaces beside mesophyll surfaces. Guard cells regulate stomatal opening, balancing carbon-dioxide uptake with water loss. Smoking damages cilia and alveolar tissue and increases risks including cancer and cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: Bulk transport connects exchange to demand
sections.body: The heart drives a double circulation through the lungs and body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure; veins return it with valves; capillaries support exchange. Red cells transport oxygen using haemoglobin, plasma carries dissolved substances and platelets contribute to clotting. Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem translocates dissolved organic nutrients between sources and sinks.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it supplies the systemic circulation at higher pressure. Valves prevent backflow when pressure differences reverse. In plants, evaporation from mesophyll surfaces and diffusion through stomata drive a transpiration stream; water is pulled through xylem. A potometer measures water uptake, which estimates rather than directly measures transpiration because some water is used elsewhere. Temperature, air movement, humidity and light can alter the rate. Explain each effect through evaporation, diffusion gradients or stomatal behaviour rather than simply saying that the plant becomes more active.

topics.tip: Arteries and veins are defined by direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content.
topics.formula: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Excretion, homeostasis and coordination

sections.heading: Keep internal conditions within limits
sections.body: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions despite external changes. Negative feedback detects a deviation and produces responses that oppose it. Temperature control balances heat loss and production: sweating cools through evaporation, and changes to skin blood flow alter heat transfer. Blood glucose control involves insulin and glucagon acting on processes such as glucose uptake and glycogen conversion.

sections.heading: The kidney removes wastes while conserving useful substances
sections.body: Excretion removes metabolic waste, including urea produced from excess amino acids in the liver. In a nephron, ultrafiltration moves small molecules from blood into the tubule under pressure while retaining blood cells and large proteins. Selective reabsorption recovers useful substances. ADH alters collecting-duct water permeability, helping regulate blood water concentration.

sections.heading: Responses can be electrical or chemical
sections.body: A receptor detects a stimulus. Sensory neurones carry impulses to the central nervous system, relay neurones connect pathways and motor neurones activate effectors. Synapses transmit signals chemically in one direction. Reflex pathways produce rapid protective responses. Hormones travel in blood and act on target cells. Plants respond through growth regulators such as auxin, with differing effects in roots and shoots.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption have different roles. Pressure filters small molecules, including both glucose and urea, into the nephron, while large proteins and blood cells remain in circulation. Glucose is normally reabsorbed rather than deliberately excreted. Negative feedback should be written as a causal sequence: a change is detected, a coordinating response is produced, an effector acts and the variable moves back towards its regulated range. In a reflex arc, the rapid response does not require a conscious decision, although information may also reach the brain.

topics.tip: Urea is made in the liver and excreted by the kidneys; urine is not the same as urea.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Reproduction, development and cell division

sections.heading: Two routes to a new organism
sections.body: Asexual reproduction uses one parent and produces genetically similar offspring, apart from mutation. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from gametes and creates variation. Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth, repair and some asexual reproduction. Meiosis reduces chromosome number to produce haploid gametes and contributes to variation.

sections.heading: Flowering plant reproduction
sections.body: Anthers produce pollen and the stigma receives it during pollination. A pollen tube grows toward an ovule; fertilisation fuses male and female nuclei. The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary into a fruit. Seed germination requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Pollination and fertilisation are different stages and may be separated in time.

sections.heading: Human reproduction and development
sections.body: The testes produce sperm and the ovaries produce ova. Fertilisation usually occurs in an oviduct, forming a zygote that divides and implants in the uterus. The placenta supports exchange between maternal and fetal circulations without normal direct mixing of their blood. Hormones coordinate the menstrual cycle; contraception can prevent gamete production, transport, fertilisation or implantation by different mechanisms.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An insect-pollinated flower often has features that promote contact between the insect and pollen-bearing or pollen-receiving surfaces. Wind-pollinated plants instead commonly expose anthers and have structures that catch airborne pollen. These are functional adaptations, not rules based on flower colour alone. After fertilisation, a seed contains an embryo and food reserves; water activates processes, oxygen supports respiration and temperature affects enzyme action. The placenta provides a large exchange surface, but it is not an absolute barrier to all harmful substances. Maternal and fetal blood normally remain in separate circulations.

topics.tip: A seed requires oxygen for respiration during germination, even before it has photosynthetic leaves.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: DNA, genetic crosses and evolution

sections.heading: Information is stored in base sequence
sections.body: DNA contains nucleotide bases arranged along two complementary strands. A gene is a DNA sequence that influences a product, commonly a protein. The order of bases determines the order of amino acids through the genetic code. Alleles are alternative versions of a gene. Genotype describes alleles; phenotype describes expressed characteristics shaped by genotype and environment.

sections.heading: Predict inheritance carefully
sections.body: For a simple dominant-recessive cross, specify allele symbols and parental genotypes, list gametes and combine them in a Punnett square. Probability predicts expected proportions across many offspring, not a guaranteed pattern in a small family. A recessive phenotype requires two recessive alleles in this model. Sex determination in the standard XX/XY model depends on whether the fertilising sperm carries X or Y.

sections.heading: Variation fuels natural selection
sections.body: Mutation can generate new alleles. Environmental conditions favour some heritable variants, whose carriers survive and reproduce more successfully. The advantageous alleles become more frequent over generations. Antibiotic resistance can spread when antibiotics select resistant bacteria; individual bacteria do not develop a needed mutation because they try to adapt. Selective breeding instead chooses parents for desired inherited traits.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In protein synthesis, transcription produces an RNA copy from a DNA template, and translation uses the RNA base sequence to assemble amino acids at ribosomes. A mutation may alter an amino-acid sequence, change the amount of product made or have no detectable effect. Codominance differs from simple dominance because both alleles influence the heterozygous phenotype. Polygenic characteristics are influenced by several genes and often show continuous variation, with environmental effects as well. In a pedigree, a phenotype alone may not identify a unique genotype, so state uncertainty where several allele combinations remain possible.

topics.tip: Dominant does not mean common, stronger or automatically beneficial.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Populations, feeding and environmental change

sections.heading: Energy flows; nutrients cycle
sections.body: Producers transfer light energy into biomass, and consumers obtain energy by feeding. Arrows in food chains show the direction of energy transfer. At each trophic level, energy is lost through respiration, movement, waste and uneaten material; not all biomass becomes growth in the next level. Decomposers break down organic matter and return nutrients to the environment.

sections.heading: Measure a habitat without selecting a convenient result
sections.body: Quadrats estimate abundance of stationary organisms. Use random coordinates for an unbiased area sample; use a transect to investigate a gradient. Repeat sampling and calculate a mean before scaling to a larger area. Measure relevant abiotic variables such as light, temperature, water availability and pH. Correlation between abundance and a variable does not by itself establish cause.

sections.heading: Human activity changes ecological systems
sections.body: Burning fuels and deforestation affect the carbon cycle and atmospheric greenhouse gases. Fertiliser runoff may cause eutrophication: algal growth shades submerged plants, dead biomass is decomposed and decomposer respiration reduces dissolved oxygen. Sulfur dioxide contributes to acid deposition. Conservation can protect habitats, maintain biodiversity and support sustainable resource use, but decisions may involve competing social and economic priorities.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The carbon cycle follows carbon atoms through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion. The nitrogen cycle involves a different set of transformations: fixation introduces usable nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen, decomposers release ammonium compounds, nitrifying organisms oxidise them, and denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is dissipated, while elements are recycled. A pyramid of biomass records living material at each level; it need not have the same shape as a pyramid counting organisms. Sampling conclusions should acknowledge spatial variation and the limitations of the chosen method.

topics.tip: A food-chain arrow points from the food organism toward its consumer.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Food production, biotechnology and genetic methods

sections.heading: Increase yield while considering consequences
sections.body: Greenhouses control light, temperature and carbon dioxide, but added energy and infrastructure have financial and environmental costs. Fertilisers supply mineral nutrients; biological control uses living organisms to reduce pests. Intensive livestock systems can limit movement and heat loss to improve growth efficiency, while raising welfare, disease and pollution questions that should be evaluated explicitly.

sections.heading: Use microorganisms as biological factories
sections.body: Yeast fermentation supports bread and alcoholic-drink production. Industrial fermenters maintain suitable temperature, pH, nutrients and, when needed, oxygen. Aseptic conditions reduce contamination; stirring distributes resources and heat. Pectinase can increase fruit-juice extraction and lactase can produce lactose-reduced milk. Conditions depend on the organism and desired product rather than one universal optimum.

sections.heading: Modify or copy genetic material
sections.body: Genetic engineering transfers selected genetic information between organisms, using tools such as restriction enzymes, ligase and vectors. Bacteria can be engineered to produce human insulin. Cloning generates genetically similar organisms through methods such as tissue culture or nuclear transfer. Benefits must be weighed against reduced diversity, animal welfare and unintended ecological effects. Describing a method is different from evaluating its use.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A fermenter is designed around its organism and product. Aeration is important for an aerobic process, while ethanol fermentation uses anaerobic conditions. A temperature jacket removes excess heat, and sensors allow conditions to be monitored rather than assumed. In genetic modification, a selected gene can be inserted into a vector and introduced into host cells; identifying successful transformants and controlling expression are essential steps. Clones share much genetic information, but environmental conditions and some biological details can still produce differences. Evaluation should separate evidence of a benefit from a claim that every use is equally safe or useful.

topics.tip: Genetic engineering transfers selected genetic material; selective breeding chooses parents over generations.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Particles, separation and atomic structure

sections.heading: A particle model explains state changes
sections.body: Solids have particles vibrating around fixed positions, liquids have nearby particles that can move past one another, and gases have widely spaced particles moving freely. Melting and boiling overcome attractions between particles; they do not usually split the particles into atoms. Diffusion arises from random particle movement and produces net spreading down a concentration gradient.

sections.heading: Separate physical mixtures appropriately
sections.body: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid; distillation recovers a solvent or separates liquids with different boiling behaviours. Fractional distillation uses repeated vaporisation and condensation. Paper chromatography separates substances through differing movement between stationary and mobile phases. Rf compares spot travel with solvent-front travel from the same baseline.

sections.heading: Atoms and isotopes
sections.body: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Atomic number counts protons; mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number. A neutral atom has equal proton and electron numbers. Relative atomic mass is an abundance-weighted mean. Electron arrangement explains many chemical patterns; ion formation changes electrons, leaving the nucleus unchanged.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The movement of a chromatographic spot depends on its interactions with both the stationary and mobile phases. A substance more strongly retained by the stationary phase travels less far under otherwise identical conditions. Rf values are useful for comparison only when relevant conditions match. Isotopic abundance calculations use an average of isotope masses weighted by their proportions; the result does not imply that an individual atom has a fractional number of neutrons. In a heating curve for a pure substance, a plateau marks a phase change under the idealised constant-pressure conditions, while supplied energy continues to overcome attractions.

topics.tip: A chromatography baseline is drawn in pencil and kept above the initial solvent level.
topics.formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bonding, structure and chemical formulae

sections.heading: Ionic and covalent bonds are different attractions
sections.body: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice. Covalent bonding is attraction involving nuclei and a shared pair of electrons. Metallic bonding is attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons. Balance ionic charges to write formulae; a neutral compound has no net charge, even though it contains charged ions.

sections.heading: Structure determines observable behaviour
sections.body: Giant ionic substances have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved because ions can move. Simple molecular substances often have low melting points because intermolecular attractions are weaker than their internal covalent bonds. Giant covalent structures such as diamond require many strong bonds to be broken; graphite has layers and mobile electrons. Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move through the structure.

sections.heading: Represent atoms without losing them
sections.body: A balanced equation conserves atoms of each element. Change coefficients, not chemical formulae, to balance it. State symbols distinguish solids, liquids, gases and aqueous solutions. Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer-shell electron contributions; bracket and charge ionic species correctly. For electron transfer, oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; these occur together.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For a dot-and-cross diagram, show only the required outer electrons and identify which atom contributed each shared electron. For ions, bracket the resulting ion and show its charge rather than drawing the transferred electron as a covalent bond. A small molecule can contain strong covalent bonds yet form a substance with a low boiling point because the attractions between molecules are relatively weak. Graphite conducts because some electrons are delocalised within its structure, whereas the electrons of diamond are held in its covalent bonding framework. Explain observed properties using both structure and the relevant moving or interacting particles.

topics.tip: Melting a molecular substance overcomes intermolecular attractions, not the covalent bonds inside each molecule.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Moles, concentrations and electrolysis

sections.heading: Count chemical amounts with moles
sections.body: Relative formula mass adds the relative atomic masses in a formula. Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass. Use balanced-equation coefficients as mole ratios, then convert to the required mass, volume or concentration. The limiting reactant is used up first. Percentage yield compares actual with theoretical yield; atom economy concerns the fraction of reactant mass incorporated into the desired product.

sections.heading: Concentration connects amount to volume
sections.body: For molar concentration, use concentration = moles/volume in dm³. Divide cm³ by 1000 before substitution. In gas calculations, use the molar gas volume specified by the question; the common school value at room conditions is 24 dm³ mol⁻¹. Empirical formulae follow the simplest whole-number mole ratio, not the simplest mass ratio.

sections.heading: Electricity drives a chemical change
sections.body: Electrolysis requires mobile ions. Cations move to the negative cathode, where reduction occurs; anions move to the positive anode, where oxidation occurs. A molten binary ionic compound produces its elements. In aqueous solutions, water-derived species compete, so identify the ions and the electrode rules before predicting products. In electroplating, the object to be coated is the cathode.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A limiting-reactant calculation first converts both starting amounts to moles. Divide each by its balanced-equation coefficient to compare available reaction units; the smaller value limits product formation. In electrolysis, electrons move through the external circuit and ions carry charge through the electrolyte. At an electrode, a half-equation must balance both atoms and net charge. For copper deposition, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu describes reduction. An aqueous electrolyte may generate a product from water-derived ions, so predictions must consider all relevant species and the stated electrode materials.

topics.tip: Never insert a volume in cm³ into n = cV when c is in mol dm⁻³.
topics.formula: n = m/M; c = n/V

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Periodic trends, air and water

sections.heading: The table organises electron patterns
sections.body: Elements in a group have related outer-electron arrangements and similar chemistry. Across a period the proton number increases. Group 1 metals react with water to produce hydroxides and hydrogen; reactivity generally increases down the group as the outer electron is more easily lost. Group 7 halogens form negative ions; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution.

sections.heading: Atmospheric gases have distinctive uses and tests
sections.body: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and variable water vapour. Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop in a suitable test. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy. Combustion in insufficient oxygen can produce poisonous carbon monoxide and particulates. Complete hydrocarbon combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

sections.heading: Water treatment is a sequence of processes
sections.body: Sedimentation and filtration remove suspended material; disinfection reduces harmful microorganisms. Dissolved salts may require desalination, for example through distillation or membrane methods, with energy and infrastructure costs. Pure water is a single substance; potable water is safe to drink but may contain dissolved substances. Chemical tests must distinguish an observed result from the conclusion drawn from it.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In Group 1, increasing distance and shielding make the outer electron easier to remove down the group, despite increasing nuclear charge. For halogens, the attraction for an incoming electron generally weakens down the group, so their displacement trend is opposite. When identifying gases, specify the test material and observation: a glowing splint relights in oxygen, while carbon dioxide makes limewater cloudy. Water treatment may disinfect without removing dissolved ions. Desalination and sterilisation solve different problems, and potable water does not need to be chemically pure.

topics.tip: Reactivity trends down Group 1 and Group 7 go in opposite directions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Metals, extraction and corrosion

sections.heading: Reactivity predicts competing reactions
sections.body: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound. The reactivity series also helps predict reaction with water, steam and dilute acids. Metal oxides can often be reduced by carbon if the metal is less reactive than carbon; more reactive metals generally require electrolysis of a suitable molten compound. Extraction method therefore depends on chemical reactivity and economic conditions.

sections.heading: Extraction involves chemical and practical decisions
sections.body: In iron extraction, carbon monoxide reduces iron oxide while limestone-derived material removes acidic impurities into slag. Aluminium extraction uses electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, reducing operating temperature. The carbon anodes are consumed because oxygen formed there reacts with them. Recycling metals often needs less energy than extraction from ore, but collection and sorting also have costs.

sections.heading: Rusting needs water and oxygen
sections.body: Iron corrosion can be reduced by barriers such as paint, grease or plastic. Galvanising adds a zinc coating that acts both as a barrier and as sacrificial protection. A more reactive attached metal preferentially oxidises. Alloys contain more than one element; differently sized atoms can disrupt the layers and make sliding more difficult, often increasing hardness.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alloy is not simply a mixture that must always be harder; its composition and processing determine the useful properties. For many common alloys, different atomic sizes hinder layer movement compared with a pure metal. In extraction questions, separate reduction of the metal compound from removal of impurities. In aluminium production, cryolite lowers the operating temperature of the electrolyte mixture, reducing energy demand compared with melting pure aluminium oxide. Sacrificial protection needs an electrical connection and a suitable environment for the corrosion cell; a disconnected zinc object nearby does not automatically protect iron.

topics.tip: A barrier coating and sacrificial protection are different mechanisms.

worked.question: Explain why zinc can continue protecting iron after a galvanised coating is scratched.
steps: Zinc is more reactive than iron.
The zinc preferentially oxidises and supplies electrons in the corrosion cell.
This sacrificial protection reduces oxidation of exposed iron.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Acids, salts and chemical analysis

sections.heading: Neutralisation is a reaction of ions
sections.body: Acids produce H⁺ in aqueous solution and alkalis produce OH⁻. Neutralisation forms water from these ions. Acid + metal forms a salt and hydrogen; acid + carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. Strong versus weak describes ionisation, whereas concentrated versus dilute describes amount per volume.

sections.heading: Choose the correct salt-preparation route
sections.body: For a soluble salt from an insoluble base, add excess base to warm acid, filter off unreacted solid and crystallise the filtrate. For an acid and soluble alkali, a titration identifies the reacting volumes without leaving excess reagent. An insoluble salt can be made by precipitation from two suitable soluble solutions, followed by filtration, washing and drying.

sections.heading: Observations identify substances
sections.body: Flame tests give characteristic colours for selected metal ions. Sodium hydroxide can form characteristic hydroxide precipitates with metal ions. Acidified silver nitrate tests for halides; acidified barium solution tests for sulfates. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with acid. Ammonium ions release ammonia when warmed with alkali; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue. State the reagent, conditions and actual observation.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A titration measures the volume needed for reactants to reach the required stoichiometric relation. Rinse a burette with the solution it will contain, record readings consistently, and add dropwise near the endpoint while mixing. Repeat to obtain concordant titres rather than averaging a rough result indiscriminately. For a pure salt from an acid and alkali, the measured quantities can be reacted again without indicator. Analytical observations should distinguish precipitate colour from gas evolution. Acidification in some ion tests removes interfering ions; the choice of acid must not introduce the ion being tested.

topics.tip: Do not heat a crystallising solution to complete dryness if the aim is well-formed crystals.

worked.question: Describe how to prepare pure dry copper(II) sulfate crystals from sulfuric acid and copper(II) oxide.
steps: Warm the acid gently and add copper(II) oxide until some solid remains.
Filter to remove the excess insoluble oxide.
Concentrate the filtrate, cool to crystallise, then separate and dry the crystals.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Energy changes and reaction rates

sections.heading: Follow the energy balance
sections.body: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb it. Bond breaking requires energy and bond formation releases energy. Estimate enthalpy change as total energy needed to break reactant bonds minus energy released forming product bonds. A catalyst changes activation energy but does not change the energy difference between reactants and products.

sections.heading: Use collision theory to explain a change in rate
sections.body: Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy and suitable orientation. Higher concentration or gas pressure increases collision frequency. Higher temperature increases particle speed and the fraction of collisions exceeding activation energy. Greater exposed surface area makes more particles available. A catalyst offers an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated overall.

sections.heading: Make a fair rate measurement
sections.body: Measure gas volume, mass loss or another appropriate change over time. Control other conditions and repeat trials. The slope of a quantity-time curve gives rate; a tangent gives instantaneous rate. A curve flattening means the measurable change has stopped, not that particles have stopped moving. Distinguish faster completion from a greater final quantity, which depends on reacting amounts.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In simple calorimetry, q = mcΔT estimates energy transferred to the measured liquid. To calculate a molar energy change, divide by the moles corresponding to the stated reaction basis and assign the sign from the system’s energy transfer. Heat loss to surroundings and heating the apparatus commonly reduce the measured liquid temperature change, affecting the result. A rate experiment may instead measure time for a fixed visible change; 1/time is then a comparative rate measure under the stated conditions, rather than a universal rate with units of amount per second.

topics.tip: A higher temperature is not explained only by more collisions; mention the larger fraction with enough energy.
topics.formula: ΔH ≈ energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds

worked.question: A reaction breaks bonds requiring 800 kJ mol⁻¹ and forms bonds releasing 950 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate the enthalpy change.
steps: Use energy in minus energy out.
The negative value indicates an exothermic change.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium

sections.heading: An equilibrium is still active
sections.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions. In a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Reactant and product concentrations remain constant, but are not necessarily equal. Material must not continuously escape if the equilibrium model is to remain appropriate.

sections.heading: A changed condition favours a response
sections.body: Increasing a reactant concentration tends to favour the direction consuming it. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, where the gaseous mole totals differ. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction. Use the balanced equation and the thermal direction together; a memorised slogan without the relevant details is incomplete.

sections.heading: Industry balances several objectives
sections.body: Conditions that maximise equilibrium yield may produce an impractically slow rate. Industrial choices also consider energy, equipment, separation and recycling. A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse processes and allows equilibrium to be reached sooner, but does not alter equilibrium composition at the same temperature. When evaluating operating conditions, separate yield effects from rate effects.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A change in pressure only shifts a gaseous equilibrium through this argument when the balanced sides have different gas-mole totals. Compressing an equilibrium with equal gaseous mole totals does not favour one direction by that rule. Temperature must be related to the exothermic or endothermic direction; treating temperature as just another concentration can produce a wrong conclusion. The concentration-time graph after a disturbance should settle to new constant values once equal forward and reverse rates are re-established. Those final values need not match each other or the original values.

topics.tip: A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium yield.

worked.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), explain the effect of higher pressure on equilibrium ammonia yield.
steps: There are four gaseous moles on the reactant side and two on the product side.
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous molecules.
The equilibrium shifts towards ammonia, increasing its equilibrium yield.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Crude oil, alkanes and alkenes

sections.heading: Separate a mixture before using it
sections.body: Crude oil is a mixture, mainly of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation separates fractions by different boiling ranges. Smaller molecules generally have lower boiling points and greater volatility; longer chains are generally more viscous. Fractions are mixtures with similar properties rather than single pure compounds. Complete combustion needs sufficient oxygen; incomplete combustion can create carbon monoxide and soot.

sections.heading: Homologous series organise chemical behaviour
sections.body: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon-carbon single bonds; open-chain alkanes have general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and, for one double bond in an open chain, formula CₙH₂ₙ. Alkenes undergo addition reactions. Bromine water is decolourised by a suitable unsaturated compound, providing a test for the double bond in this context.

sections.heading: Cracking changes the product balance
sections.body: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, often including an alkane and an alkene, using heat and an appropriate catalyst or other specified conditions. It supplies useful fuels and chemical feedstocks. Balance atoms in any proposed equation. Structural formulae show bonding and can distinguish structural isomers, which share a molecular formula but have different connectivity.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A homologous series shares a functional pattern and general formula while successive members differ by a CH₂ unit. Chain length changes physical properties gradually, while the functional group strongly influences reaction type. Alkanes can react with halogens by substitution under suitable light conditions; alkenes undergo addition at a carbon-carbon double bond. A displayed or structural formula must show a chemically valid bonding arrangement, with carbon making four bonds in the usual neutral structures. Two compounds with the same molecular formula can have different connectivity and therefore be structural isomers.

topics.tip: A cracking equation must balance both carbon and hydrogen atoms.

worked.question: Complete the cracking equation C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ___.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Alcohols, acids, esters and polymers

sections.heading: Functional groups change behaviour
sections.body: Alcohols contain the −OH functional group; carboxylic acids contain −COOH. Ethanol can be made by fermentation of sugars using yeast under suitable anaerobic conditions, or by adding steam to ethene using an appropriate catalyst and industrial conditions. Oxidising ethanol can form ethanoic acid. Describing an alcohol as simply a hydrocarbon is incorrect because it also contains oxygen.

sections.heading: Esterification links an acid to an alcohol
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can react to form an ester and water, usually with acid catalysis and warming. Ester names combine the alcohol-derived alkyl group with the acid-derived carboxylate group. Many esters have useful aromas or solvent properties. Conditions, separation and equilibrium affect practical yield; the reaction equation alone does not describe a complete manufacturing process.

sections.heading: Small molecules become macromolecules
sections.body: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening their carbon-carbon double bonds. The repeating unit must preserve every atom of the monomer, with continuation bonds through brackets. Condensation polymerisation links monomers with suitable functional groups and eliminates a small molecule. Disposal choices include reuse, recycling and energy recovery, each with limitations including sorting, contamination, emissions and persistence.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: To draw an addition-polymer repeat unit, retain the monomer’s side groups, change the double bond to a single bond and show continuation bonds through both sides of the brackets. A condensation polymer has linking groups related to its monomers’ functional groups and forms a small molecule in the linking reaction. A polymer can be chemically resistant yet difficult to recycle because of mixed grades, additives or contamination. In ethanol production, compare fermentation and hydration using feedstock, purity, conditions, rate and separation rather than assuming one method is best under every industrial constraint.

topics.tip: In addition polymerisation the monomer’s atoms remain in the polymer repeat unit.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Motion graphs and acceleration

sections.heading: Describe change with quantities and directions
sections.body: Distance measures total path length, while displacement is change in position with direction. Speed is distance divided by time; velocity includes direction. Average speed uses total distance divided by total time. Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time and can describe a change of direction even if speed is constant.

sections.heading: Gradients and areas have physical meanings
sections.body: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement. A flat velocity-time section represents constant velocity, whereas a flat displacement-time section represents rest. Use a tangent to estimate a gradient at a particular instant on a curve, showing the triangle used.

sections.heading: Uniform acceleration is a restricted model
sections.body: For constant acceleration, v = u + at and v² = u² + 2as. Choose the equation that contains your known quantities and the desired unknown. State a positive direction before substituting signed values. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Stopping distance combines thinking and braking distances; fatigue, speed and road conditions affect different stages.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A curved displacement-time graph has a changing gradient and therefore changing velocity. A straight sloping velocity-time segment represents uniform acceleration, even if the velocity itself is negative. For a journey with several stages, add the distances and times before calculating average speed. In experimental motion work, light gates or video measurements reduce some timing limitations, but the physical quantity still depends on gate spacing, flag length or scale calibration. State the model assumptions when applying constant-acceleration equations, because a single average acceleration does not prove the acceleration was uniform throughout.

topics.tip: A descending velocity-time line can indicate slowing down or speeding up in the negative direction; examine the sign.
topics.formula: a = (v − u)/t; v² = u² + 2as

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Forces, moments, momentum and springs

sections.heading: Resultant force changes motion
sections.body: Force is a vector. A zero resultant force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. For a constant mass, F = ma. Weight is the gravitational force mg, whereas mass measures the amount of matter and resistance to acceleration. Free-body diagrams show forces on one object; action-reaction pairs act on different objects.

sections.heading: Turning and balancing
sections.body: A moment is force multiplied by perpendicular distance to the pivot. For rotational equilibrium, clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. A body’s centre of gravity is where its weight can be treated as acting. Stability depends on the centre of gravity and the support base. A spring follows F = kx only within its linear range; extension is the increase from original length.

sections.heading: Momentum accounts for interactions
sections.body: Momentum is mass × velocity. In an isolated interaction, total momentum is conserved. A resultant force equals rate of change of momentum; increasing collision time can reduce mean force for the same momentum change. During terminal fall, resistive force grows until it balances weight and acceleration becomes zero. Energy transfers may still continue while terminal speed is maintained.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For an object in equilibrium, both the resultant force and resultant moment must be zero. Balancing moments about a convenient pivot removes the moment of any force acting through that pivot, but the force still matters in the overall force balance. A spring constant is the gradient of a force-extension graph in the linear range. The area under that graph is elastic energy transferred; for a linear spring this is ½Fx = ½kx². In a collision, use one positive direction consistently before applying conservation of momentum.

topics.tip: Use a signed velocity change when an object reverses direction.
topics.formula: moment = F × perpendicular distance; p = mv; F = Δp/Δt

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Charge, current, voltage and circuit rules

sections.heading: Current is moving charge
sections.body: Charge flow is Q = It. Current has the same value through components in series; currents entering a junction sum to those leaving. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. In parallel branches the potential difference is equal. An ammeter is placed in series and a voltmeter in parallel with the component being measured.

sections.heading: Components respond differently
sections.body: An ohmic resistor has constant resistance at constant temperature. A filament lamp’s resistance increases as its temperature rises. A diode conducts much more readily in one direction. The resistance of a thermistor commonly decreases as temperature rises; an LDR’s resistance decreases as light level rises. Interpret each component using its current-voltage behaviour, not by assuming every graph is a straight line.

sections.heading: Resistance and power in networks
sections.body: For series resistors, add resistances. Parallel paths reduce the total resistance compared with any individual branch. V = IR relates a component’s potential difference, current and resistance. Electrical power is P = VI and, for a resistive component, P = I²R. Energy transferred is E = Pt. Match units: watts and seconds give joules.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: In parallel branches, equal potential difference does not imply equal current unless the branch resistances are equal. For two resistors, the reciprocal relation 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ gives a combined resistance below either individual resistance. In a potential divider, the fraction of supply voltage across a series component depends on its share of the total resistance. Measurements must distinguish a component’s current-voltage behaviour from changes caused by heating. Connect equipment correctly and keep current low enough to avoid unwanted temperature changes when investigating an ohmic resistor.

topics.tip: Current is not used up as it travels around a circuit.
topics.formula: Q = It; V = IR; P = VI; E = Pt

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Mains safety and static electricity

sections.heading: Protect the user when something goes wrong
sections.body: A live conductor is at an alternating potential relative to earth; neutral provides the return path. An earth conductor connects exposed conducting parts to earth so a fault can create a large current and operate protective devices. A fuse melts when excessive current heats it. Double-insulated equipment has appropriate insulating barriers and does not rely on an earth wire for exposed metal protection.

sections.heading: Choose protective ratings sensibly
sections.body: Calculate normal current from P/V before choosing the next suitable fuse rating above it, allowing for the specified equipment characteristics. Overloading sockets can overheat wiring. Electrical energy billing commonly uses kilowatt-hours: multiply power in kilowatts by time in hours. A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit, not power per hour.

sections.heading: Charge transfer creates static effects
sections.body: Rubbing insulating materials can transfer electrons. Losing electrons leaves a positive charge; gaining them leaves a negative charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can attract a neutral object by redistributing its charges. Static build-up may cause sparks, so fuel handling and other sensitive processes use earthing and suitable precautions.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An alternating supply reverses direction repeatedly; a direct supply has a fixed direction. A fuse is chosen to tolerate normal operation while protecting against excessive current in a suitable circuit. The live path must be interrupted by the protective or switching device where specified, because leaving internal parts connected to live can remain dangerous. Static induction redistributes charges within a nearby object without requiring net charge transfer to it. When a conductor is earthed, electrons may flow to or from Earth according to the surrounding charge arrangement.

topics.tip: An earth wire is a fault-protection route; it should not normally carry the appliance current.
