topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Wave behaviour, sound and the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.heading: Track the oscillation and the energy separately
sections.body: Waves transfer energy without net transport of the medium. In transverse waves the oscillation is perpendicular to travel; in longitudinal waves it is parallel. Amplitude measures maximum displacement, wavelength measures repeat distance, frequency counts cycles per second and period is time per cycle. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

sections.heading: At boundaries, follow what changes
sections.body: Reflection returns a wave from a boundary; refraction occurs when wave speed changes between media. Frequency remains fixed by the source during refraction, while wavelength changes. Diffraction spreads waves around obstacles or through openings and is greatest when wavelength and opening width are comparable. Sound needs a medium; pitch relates to frequency and loudness to amplitude.

sections.heading: One spectrum, different interactions
sections.body: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and have the same speed in vacuum. Increasing frequency runs from radio through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma radiation. Use depends on penetration, absorption and energy transfer. Ionising radiation can damage cells; exposure decisions weigh dose, shielding, distance and benefits. Infrared is associated with thermal emission and absorption, not with a special category of heat particles.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: At a boundary, a wave’s frequency remains controlled by its source, so a speed change produces a corresponding wavelength change. Echo measurements use a return journey: divide the product of speed and time by two to find the reflecting distance. Increasing sound amplitude generally increases loudness; increasing frequency raises pitch. Different electromagnetic bands interact differently with matter, which explains uses such as radio communication, thermal imaging and medical imaging. The label ionising concerns sufficient energy to remove bound electrons in relevant interactions, not simply whether a wave travels through a solid.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Refraction, total internal reflection and lenses

sections.heading: Draw from the normal
sections.body: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal, not the surface. A ray entering a slower medium generally bends towards the normal; entering a faster medium generally bends away. The refractive index compares speeds and, for air-to-material geometry, relates sin i to sin r. Keep calculator angles in degrees for school ray calculations.

sections.heading: A critical angle sets a boundary
sections.body: Total internal reflection requires travel from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index medium and an incidence angle greater than the critical angle. At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Optical fibres use repeated internal reflection, although real systems also have attenuation and manufacturing constraints. Reflection below the critical angle is not total internal reflection.

sections.heading: Lenses produce images by ray geometry
sections.body: A converging lens brings parallel rays towards a focal point. Draw a ray parallel to the principal axis that passes through the far focus and a ray through the optical centre that continues essentially undeviated in the thin-lens model. Where real rays meet, a real image forms; where their backward extensions meet, the image is virtual. Magnification is image size divided by object size.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A real image can be formed on a screen because light rays actually converge there. A virtual image is located where backward extensions of rays meet, and cannot be projected directly onto a screen in the same way. A converging lens can form either type depending on object position. Ray diagrams must use a clear principal axis and accurately placed focal points. At total internal reflection, the critical-angle condition concerns a higher-index to lower-index boundary; simply making any incidence angle large does not guarantee it.

topics.tip: Total internal reflection cannot occur when the ray first enters a higher-index medium from air.
topics.formula: n = sin i/sin r; sin c = 1/n for a material-to-air boundary

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Energy transfers, work, power and resources

sections.heading: Energy accounting must balance
sections.body: Energy can be stored kinetically, gravitationally, elastically, thermally, chemically and in other ways. It transfers through mechanical work, electrical work, heating and radiation. The total is conserved, even when useful energy spreads into less useful thermal stores. Work done by a constant force parallel to displacement is W = Fd. Power measures energy transfer per second.

sections.heading: Calculate the change, not an unrelated total
sections.body: Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy change is mgΔh near Earth’s surface. Efficiency is useful output divided by total input, expressed as a fraction or percentage. A machine can have high power and low efficiency; these quantities answer different questions. Reduce unwanted transfers through insulation, lubrication or appropriate material choices.

sections.heading: Evaluate resources in context
sections.body: Fossil fuels are energy-dense but finite and produce emissions. Nuclear generation has low operational carbon emissions but creates radioactive waste and needs substantial infrastructure. Wind and solar are renewable but variable; hydroelectric and other storage schemes can help balance demand. Compare reliability, output, environmental impacts and cost over the system’s lifetime rather than using renewable as a synonym for impact-free.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Work requires displacement with a component along the force direction. A force can be present without doing mechanical work on a stationary object through that force’s application point. An energy-flow diagram should account for the entire input and define the useful output for the task. In transmission systems, raising voltage reduces current for a given power, lowering I²R losses; this does not mean voltage itself is energy. For resource comparisons, define the intended demand pattern and compare lifecycle impacts, reliability and storage needs rather than only fuel availability.

topics.tip: Efficiency cannot exceed 100% for the stated energy input-output boundary.
topics.formula: Eₖ = ½mv²; ΔEₚ = mgΔh; P = E/t

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Density, pressure and thermal changes

sections.heading: Density relates material amount to volume
sections.body: Density is mass divided by volume. Use a balance and appropriate volume measurement: regular dimensions for a block, displacement for a suitable irregular solid. Keep units consistent; 1 g/cm³ equals 1000 kg/m³. Pressure is force per area, so the same force produces greater pressure on a smaller area.

sections.heading: Particles explain liquid and gas pressure
sections.body: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and density: Δp = ρgΔh. Gas pressure arises from particle collisions with surfaces. At constant temperature for a fixed mass, pressure times volume remains constant in the ideal-gas approximation used here. Kelvin temperature begins at absolute zero; convert Celsius by adding about 273. State which quantities remain fixed in any gas-law problem.

sections.heading: Heating can raise temperature or change state
sections.body: Specific heat capacity relates energy to mass and temperature rise. Specific latent heat relates energy to mass changed between phases without a temperature rise during the idealised phase change. During melting or boiling, supplied energy changes particle arrangement rather than increasing mean kinetic energy. Conduction, convection and radiation are different transfer mechanisms, each favoured by different materials and conditions.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Pressure in a liquid depends on depth below the surface, liquid density and gravitational field strength, not on the total amount of liquid in a particular vessel. For a gas-law comparison, keep the gas mass fixed and identify whether temperature or volume is constant. Heating a solid or liquid may cause expansion, while a phase change absorbs or releases latent energy without the same temperature response. In a heating experiment, insulation reduces losses, but measurements may also need to account for the container, heater and thermometer response.

topics.tip: A temperature change of 20°C is a change of 20 K; an absolute temperature of 20°C is about 293 K.
topics.formula: ρ = m/V; p = F/A; E = mcΔT; E = mL

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Magnetic fields, motors and induction

sections.heading: Fields represent force patterns
sections.body: Magnetic field lines outside a magnet run from north to south. Their direction is the direction a north test pole would move, and closer spacing indicates a stronger field. A current in a wire produces a magnetic field; a coil concentrates it, and a suitable iron core strengthens an electromagnet. Field direction depends on current direction.

sections.heading: A current can produce motion
sections.body: A current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field can experience a force. The force is greatest when current and field are perpendicular and becomes zero when they are parallel. Fleming’s left-hand rule relates field, conventional current and force. Motors use forces on a coil to create a turning effect, with appropriate switching to maintain rotation.

sections.heading: Changing flux can produce a voltage
sections.body: Moving a magnet relative to a coil or changing the field through it can induce an emf. Faster change, stronger fields and more turns can increase the effect. The induced current opposes the change that produces it. Transformers use changing magnetic flux to transfer energy between coils; their simple operating model requires alternating input. A higher transmission voltage lowers current for the same power and reduces resistive losses.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Induction depends on changing magnetic flux linkage, not on the simple presence of a magnetic field. Reversing the motion or magnetic orientation reverses the induced voltage direction in the usual arrangement. A motor transfers electrical energy into mechanical work; a generator transfers mechanical work into electrical energy. For an ideal transformer, voltage follows turns ratio and input power equals output power, so increasing voltage decreases current. Real transformers have losses, so an efficiency statement must use the actual input and output powers.

topics.tip: A stationary magnet beside a stationary coil does not continuously induce an emf.
topics.formula: Vₚ/Vₛ = Nₚ/Nₛ; ideal input power = output power

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Radioactivity, half-life and nuclear reactions

sections.heading: Unstable nuclei change spontaneously
sections.body: Alpha radiation is a helium nucleus; beta-minus radiation is an electron emitted when a neutron changes to a proton; gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation from nuclear de-excitation. Their penetration and ionising powers differ. Nuclear equations conserve charge number and nucleon number. Radioactive decay is random for an individual nucleus but predictable statistically for a large population.

sections.heading: Use background-corrected measurements
sections.body: Activity measures decays per second in becquerels. A detector records a count rate that also depends on geometry and efficiency. Subtract background before analysing decay. A half-life is the time for activity, or number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. After n half-lives the remaining fraction is (1/2)ⁿ. A graph may need repeated halving rather than a single chosen interval.

sections.heading: Applications involve a risk-benefit choice
sections.body: Contamination introduces radioactive material into or onto something; irradiation exposes it to radiation without necessarily leaving radioactive material behind. Shielding, distance and short handling times reduce exposure. Fission splits heavy nuclei and can sustain a chain reaction; fusion combines light nuclei and requires extreme conditions. Nuclear energy releases involve a small decrease in total rest mass, not a failure of mass-energy conservation.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The range of emitted radiation is different from the half-life of its source. Range describes travel through a material, whereas half-life describes the statistical decrease in undecayed nuclei over time. In beta-minus decay, nucleon number remains unchanged while proton number rises by one. In alpha decay, nucleon number falls by four and proton number by two. Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing either number. Repeated background-corrected measurements and suitable counting times reduce the relative influence of random fluctuations, but they do not make individual decays predictable.

topics.tip: Subtract background before halving; add it back only if the measured total is requested.

worked.question: A source gives 820 counts/min including a steady 20 counts/min background. Find the expected total count rate after three half-lives.
steps: The initial corrected source count rate is 820 − 20 = 800 counts/min.
After three half-lives it is 800/8 = 100 counts/min.
Add background again: expected measured rate = 120 counts/min.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Orbits, stars and the expanding universe

sections.heading: Gravity continually changes orbital direction
sections.body: A planet or satellite in a circular orbit accelerates because its velocity direction changes. Gravity supplies the centripetal resultant force. The period is the time for one orbit; speed in a circular orbit is circumference divided by period. Use consistent radius and time units. Natural and artificial satellites can have different orbital purposes, altitudes and periods.

sections.heading: Stars evolve according to mass
sections.body: A star forms when gravity compresses gas and dust until fusion becomes established. During the main sequence, inward gravity balances outward pressure supported by energy release. Lower-mass and higher-mass stars follow different later stages. A Sun-like star can become a red giant and then leave a white dwarf; much more massive stars can undergo supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes.

sections.heading: Evidence supports a developing cosmological model
sections.body: Spectral redshift from distant galaxies is interpreted as evidence of recession in the expanding-universe model. More distant galaxies generally show larger recession velocities on large scales. The cosmic microwave background is another major piece of evidence for an early hot dense universe. Models depend on observations and can be refined; expansion does not imply that every gravitationally bound object is itself expanding.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A circular orbit can have constant speed while its velocity changes continuously because direction changes. A star’s luminosity is its total emitted power, whereas apparent brightness also depends on distance. A spectrum contains lines associated with particular atomic transitions; shifting the pattern towards longer wavelengths supports a recession interpretation in the relevant astronomical model. Stellar mass strongly influences the later stages of evolution. A scientific explanation of the universe should connect observations to a model and recognise the distinction between directly measured spectra and quantities inferred using assumptions.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: CPU architecture and embedded systems

sections.heading: A stored program is fetched and executed
sections.body: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction, decodes it and executes its operation. The control unit coordinates these activities; the ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations. Registers hold small amounts of immediately needed data or addresses. In the von Neumann model, instructions and data share memory. The program counter identifies the next instruction, while other registers support memory access and intermediate results.

sections.heading: Performance has several bottlenecks
sections.body: A higher clock frequency can increase cycles per second, but does not guarantee an equal increase in overall program speed. Cache keeps frequently used information close to the processor. Additional cores can execute suitable tasks concurrently, but software must support effective parallel work. Compare CPUs using the task, memory behaviour, power and architecture rather than one headline figure.

sections.heading: Embedded systems have a focused job
sections.body: An embedded system is a computer integrated into another device for a particular function. Examples include a washing-machine controller, engine management system and thermostat. They often have constrained memory, input/output and power requirements, and may need dependable real-time responses. A general-purpose computer instead runs a wider range of applications chosen by the user.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: The program counter stores the address of the next instruction rather than the instruction itself. The memory address register identifies a memory location, while the memory data register holds data being transferred. The accumulator can hold intermediate ALU results. These roles explain the difference between an address and its contents without requiring a hardware-level account of every signal transfer. An embedded controller is chosen for its specified response, inputs and outputs. A suitable answer explains why a constrained, dependable purpose-built system fits the device rather than merely naming a household appliance.

topics.tip: Clock speed measures cycles per second, not completed user tasks per second.

worked.question: Explain two reasons why doubling a CPU’s core count may not double the speed of a program.
steps: Some instructions or program stages depend on earlier results and cannot run concurrently.
The program may not be written to divide its work effectively across cores.
Memory, input/output or coordination overhead may limit overall performance.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Memory, secondary storage and file sizes

sections.heading: Primary memory and persistent storage serve different roles
sections.body: RAM stores programs and data currently in use and is volatile. ROM is non-volatile and stores instructions needed for tasks such as starting a device. Cache is small, fast memory used to reduce CPU waiting. Virtual memory uses secondary storage to support memory management when RAM is insufficient, but access is slower and excessive swapping reduces performance.

sections.heading: Choose storage for its context
sections.body: Magnetic, optical and solid-state storage differ in access speed, capacity, portability, durability and cost. Solid-state devices have no moving read mechanism and are useful in portable equipment; magnetic storage can offer high capacity at a competitive cost. A justification should connect a property to the actual user need. Non-volatile does not mean immune to corruption, damage or accidental deletion.

sections.heading: Translate representations into storage requirements
sections.body: A bit has two values, a nibble is four bits and a byte is eight bits. Follow the conversion convention specified in the question. Uncompressed image size depends on pixel dimensions and colour depth; sound size depends on sample rate, bit depth, duration and channels. Include metadata or compression only if supplied. More samples or greater depth can improve fidelity but increase storage demand.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Virtual memory does not physically expand RAM. The operating system moves data between main memory and secondary storage to manage available memory, with slower access when needed data is not in RAM. For sound-file calculations, include channel count only when the question specifies it; a stereo recording normally stores two sampled channels. State any metadata or unit convention assumed. A storage recommendation should link a required characteristic, such as portability or durability, to a user scenario. A list of device names without those links does not justify a choice.

topics.tip: Convert bits to bytes once, and state whether your answer includes metadata.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Binary, hexadecimal and digital representation

sections.heading: Represent whole numbers using place value
sections.body: An unsigned eight-bit value uses places 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, giving a range from 0 to 255. Binary addition follows carry rules; a carry beyond the available width causes overflow in the unsigned model. Hexadecimal uses digits 0–9 and A–F; each hex digit corresponds to four bits, making binary values easier to read.

sections.heading: Text and images need agreed encodings
sections.body: A character set maps characters to numerical codes. ASCII covers a relatively small set, while Unicode supports many writing systems and symbols. The number of available codes depends on the encoding’s allocated bits, but real Unicode encodings can use differing byte lengths. Bitmap images store pixel colours; greater resolution or colour depth generally increases file size and may improve detail.

sections.heading: Sampling and compression make trade-offs
sections.body: Sound sampling measures amplitude at regular intervals. A higher sampling frequency captures more temporal detail, and greater bit depth provides more amplitude levels. Lossless compression allows exact reconstruction, useful for text and program code. Lossy compression discards selected information to reduce size further, useful when a controlled quality loss is acceptable. Compression does not always reduce every input file.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An unsigned eight-bit system cannot represent every result of adding two eight-bit values. For example, 200 + 100 is 300, beyond its maximum 255, so a fixed-width representation overflows. A left shift can multiply by two only while the intended value remains within range; bits shifted out are lost. Character encoding, image pixels and sampled sound all map information into binary, but their interpretations differ. Lossless compression is required when reconstructing every original program instruction or text character matters. A smaller lossy media file is not an exact copy of its original data.

topics.tip: A binary shift can lose bits at the fixed-width boundary; it is not always a safe multiplication.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Networks, addressing, protocols and layers

sections.heading: Networks share resources and communication
sections.body: A LAN covers a limited organisational or geographical area; a WAN connects networks over wider distances. A switch directs traffic within a network and a router forwards traffic between networks. Wireless access points connect wireless devices. Network performance depends on available bandwidth, connected devices, transmission conditions and the service being used, not just whether the connection is wired.

sections.heading: Addresses and protocols support delivery
sections.body: A MAC address identifies a network interface at the local-link level; an IP address supports routing between networks. DNS resolves human-readable domain names into address information. Protocols are agreed communication rules: HTTP/HTTPS support web communication, and email protocols perform sending and retrieval roles. Encryption in HTTPS protects data in transit; it does not prove a website’s content is truthful.

sections.heading: Layers reduce dependence between tasks
sections.body: A layered model separates concerns such as application communication and transmission. Each layer provides services to the layer above and follows agreed interfaces. Standardisation helps equipment and software from different organisations interoperate and makes faults easier to isolate. Client-server networks centralise services and management; peer-to-peer arrangements distribute sharing without the same dedicated-server structure.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A router’s role is to forward traffic between networks; a switch directs local network traffic using information appropriate to its layer. DNS makes addressing easier for people by resolving names, but it does not store the entire content of the requested website. Protocol layering allows one implementation to change while compatible interfaces remain stable. Distinguish bandwidth from measured performance: a high-bandwidth link can still be slow because of congestion, latency, interference, a busy server or another bottleneck. Client-server management can simplify accounts and backups but also creates dependencies requiring availability planning.

topics.tip: The internet is infrastructure; the World Wide Web is one service using it.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Threats, prevention and layered defence

sections.heading: Identify the mechanism of the threat
sections.body: Malware includes programs designed for harmful or unauthorised activity. Phishing and other social engineering manipulate people into revealing information or taking unsafe actions. Brute-force attacks try many credentials. A denial-of-service attack exhausts resources so legitimate users cannot obtain service. SQL injection exploits unsafe handling of data in database queries; it is not prevented simply by making a password longer.

sections.heading: Match each control to a threat
sections.body: Access controls restrict what authenticated users can do. Strong unique passwords and suitable account protections reduce credential risks. Anti-malware tools detect known or suspicious software, while updates close discovered vulnerabilities. Firewalls filter network traffic according to rules. Encryption protects confidentiality when keys are managed correctly; it does not itself prevent deletion or validate the accuracy of stored data.

sections.heading: Plan for failure as well as prevention
sections.body: Backups support recovery after loss or corruption. Keep appropriate separate copies, test restoration and control who can alter them. Staff training and clear procedures complement technical controls. Penetration testing explores weaknesses with authorisation and an agreed scope. A sound answer links the proposed measure to the scenario rather than claiming any single tool makes a system completely secure.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Defence should cover prevention, detection and recovery. A firewall can block specified traffic but does not replace patching a vulnerable application. Password hashing is not the same as encrypting passwords for later recovery: a suitable password-verification design avoids needing to retrieve the original password. Backups must be protected from the same event that damages the main copy, and restoration should be tested. In scenario questions, name the specific threat, explain how the control interrupts it and identify a realistic limitation rather than claiming that one control eliminates every risk.

topics.tip: Authentication verifies identity; authorisation controls permitted actions.

Multi-factor authentication and appropriate filtering can reduce the chance that stolen passwords alone compromise accounts.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Operating systems, utilities and translators

sections.heading: The operating system manages shared resources
sections.body: An operating system provides a user interface and coordinates memory, processes, peripherals, files and users. Memory management allocates available memory and prevents inappropriate interference between processes. Device drivers let the system communicate with hardware through suitable interfaces. File management organises names, locations and access permissions; user management establishes accounts and privileges.

sections.heading: Utilities support maintenance
sections.body: Encryption utilities protect data confidentiality, compression utilities reduce representations where possible, and backup utilities support recovery. Defragmentation can improve access patterns on some magnetic disks by reorganising fragmented files; it is not a general performance remedy for solid-state storage. A utility should be chosen for the actual storage and maintenance problem.

sections.heading: Translate source into executable operations
sections.body: A compiler translates a program into another form before execution, commonly producing object or executable code. An interpreter executes through a runtime by translating or processing instructions during execution. An assembler translates assembly language. An IDE supports writing, running and debugging with tools such as syntax highlighting, error diagnostics and breakpoints. No translator proves that the program meets its user requirements.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A process can be ready to run yet waiting because the operating system shares limited processor time between tasks. Memory management allocates resources and helps isolate programs. Device drivers translate the operating system’s requests into the appropriate device interface. Compilation and interpretation are implementation strategies rather than measures of program quality; either can execute a logically incorrect program. A compiler may report syntax errors before execution, but it cannot generally establish that every user requirement is met. Choose utility software based on the actual maintenance task and storage technology.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Ethics, legislation and environmental decisions

sections.heading: A legal action can still raise an ethical problem
sections.body: Evaluate stakeholders, benefits, harms and alternatives in a computing decision. Privacy, surveillance, accessibility, inclusion and algorithmic bias may affect different groups unequally. A reasoned judgement connects evidence to the scenario and acknowledges a genuine trade-off, rather than listing disconnected advantages and disadvantages.

sections.heading: Understand the purpose of relevant legislation
sections.body: In UK computing contexts, data protection law controls handling of personal data; computer misuse law concerns unauthorised access and related misuse; copyright law protects qualifying works; software licences define permitted uses. Name the relevant law or licence where the course requires it and relate it to the conduct in the question. Consent is not the only possible lawful basis for every personal-data use.

sections.heading: Consider the whole life cycle
sections.body: Equipment manufacture requires energy and materials, use consumes power and disposal creates waste. Repair, reuse, longer product lifetimes and responsible recycling can reduce some impacts. Cloud services still rely on physical infrastructure. Open-source and proprietary licensing provide different permissions and responsibilities; free of charge is not the same as open source, and either model may include commercial services.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A balanced evaluation should identify stakeholders who gain convenience, cost savings or access, and stakeholders who may face exclusion, surveillance or error. An automated decision can reproduce bias in its training data or design. Accessibility includes suitable interaction for users with differing needs, not just whether a device is inexpensive. Software licensing distinguishes permissions to inspect, modify and redistribute from the question of price. Environmental claims should consider manufacturing, running energy, repair and disposal; moving a service to a remote data centre changes where impacts occur rather than eliminating them.

topics.tip: For exam revision, focus on the principle and scenario; current legal interpretation requires authoritative guidance.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Decomposition, searches, sorts and trace tables

sections.heading: Make a problem small enough to reason about
sections.body: Decomposition divides a problem into manageable subproblems. Abstraction retains relevant details and removes irrelevant ones. An algorithm is a finite, ordered description of how to solve a defined problem. Inputs, outputs and preconditions should be clear. A trace table records values as instructions execute; update a value only when the corresponding instruction runs.

sections.heading: Search depends on the data arrangement
sections.body: Linear search checks items in sequence and works without sorting. Binary search compares with a middle value and discards one half repeatedly, requiring sorted data. Be explicit about first and last positions and how the middle is rounded. A search must handle the item-not-found case and terminate even on an empty or one-item range.

sections.heading: Sorting algorithms do different work
sections.body: Bubble sort compares neighbouring values and swaps those out of order over repeated passes. Insertion sort inserts each new value into a growing sorted region. Merge sort splits the data, sorts smaller parts and merges them in order. Show the state after the precise pass or merge requested; a correct final ordering alone may not demonstrate the specified method.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: For binary search, write down the current search boundaries and update them so the already-tested middle value is excluded when appropriate. This guarantees progress towards termination. A trace table should reflect the algorithm as written, including loop conditions and update order. For insertion sort, the sorted region grows as the next value is inserted in its correct position; for bubble sort, repeated adjacent swaps move values through a pass. A final sorted list does not show which algorithm produced it, so intermediate states matter when a method is specified.

topics.tip: An algorithm description should include what happens when no matching item exists.

worked.question: Why does binary search fail as a general method on unsorted data?
steps: Its decision discards a half based on comparison with a middle value.
Without ordering, smaller or larger values may appear in either half.
The target can therefore be discarded even when present.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Programming constructs, data types and subprograms

sections.heading: Control execution deliberately
sections.body: Sequence performs instructions in order. Selection chooses a path using a condition. Iteration repeats work through count-controlled or condition-controlled loops. Variables store values that may change; constants represent fixed named values. Choose integer, real, Boolean, character or string types to fit the meaning and required operations. Input normally needs conversion and validation before numerical use.

sections.heading: Use collections and files appropriately
sections.body: Arrays store indexed elements, and two-dimensional arrays organise a grid of values. Check index boundaries and whether the language starts at zero or one. String operations include length, slicing and searching, with language-specific details. File handling needs opening, reading or writing and closing using appropriate modes; a program should handle missing files and invalid input where required.

sections.heading: Subprograms make interfaces explicit
sections.body: A function returns a value; a procedure performs a task without a required returned value in the exam model. Parameters pass data through the interface. Local variables reduce unintended interference, while global state can create hidden dependencies. Testing a subprogram separately helps isolate faults. Meaningful identifiers and clear modular structure support maintainability better than comments that merely repeat each line.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A count-controlled loop is convenient when the number of repetitions is known; a condition-controlled loop suits input validation or work with an unknown number of items. Initialisation must occur at the correct scope: reset a total before processing a new dataset, not inside the loop that accumulates it. Parameters make a subprogram’s required inputs explicit. A returned value must be stored or used by the caller if later computation needs it. For arrays and strings, check both valid index limits and the behaviour on empty input rather than assuming every collection contains an item.

topics.tip: Check whether a loop’s final value is inclusive before counting its iterations.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Validation, defensive design and testing

sections.heading: Reject invalid input for a specific reason
sections.body: Validation checks whether input satisfies rules such as range, length, type, presence or format. It does not establish truth: a plausible but incorrect birth date can pass a range check. Verification checks a copy against an original, for example through double entry or visual comparison. Authentication establishes who a user is; access rules then govern what they may do.

sections.heading: Plan tests around meaningful boundaries
sections.body: Normal test data represents acceptable typical input. Boundary data probes edges of allowed ranges, including values just outside them where appropriate. Invalid data should be rejected safely. State the expected result before testing; otherwise an observed output has no standard of comparison. Include zero, empty inputs, duplicates and missing records when they are relevant to the program’s contract.

sections.heading: Separate finding an error from explaining it
sections.body: A syntax error violates language rules; a logic error produces incorrect behaviour despite valid syntax. Runtime problems arise during execution. Use trace tables, breakpoints and focused tests to locate the first incorrect state. Correct one cause and rerun affected tests. Defensive design should keep user data intact when an operation fails rather than falsely reporting that it succeeded.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A boundary test should state an input and its expected output or rejection. For an inclusive range 1–10, 0, 1, 10 and 11 check both permitted edges and their immediate outside neighbours. Verification compares copied data with an original; validation checks conformity to rules. Neither necessarily proves that a claimed real-world fact is true. A test plan should include normal operation as well as relevant failure cases such as an unavailable file or empty collection. When saving fails, retain the user’s unsaved work and explain the failure instead of falsely confirming completion.

topics.tip: “The program runs” is not an expected result; state the required output or rejection.

worked.question: An age field accepts integers from 11 to 18 inclusive. Propose a focused boundary test set.
steps: Use the lower boundary and neighbour: 10 and 11.
Use the upper boundary and neighbour: 18 and 19.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Boolean expressions and truth tables

sections.heading: Logic operates on true and false
sections.body: AND is true only when both inputs are true. OR is true when at least one input is true. NOT reverses its input. Use brackets to show the intended grouping of a compound expression. A condition such as age ≥ 11 AND age ≤ 18 expresses an inclusive range; replacing AND with OR would accept many invalid values.

sections.heading: Enumerate the whole input space
sections.body: A truth table for n independent Boolean inputs has 2ⁿ rows. List combinations systematically to avoid omission, calculate intermediate columns, then evaluate the final expression. Logic diagrams and expressions must represent the same connection structure. A negation over a complete expression applies after evaluating that expression, not separately to whichever symbol is visually nearby.

sections.heading: Use logic to explain program behaviour
sections.body: Comparisons produce Boolean results and can be combined in selections and loops. A loop condition describes when to continue or stop according to the construct being used. Test both outcomes and important combinations. Redundant checks can sometimes be simplified, but clarity and correctness take priority over making the expression short.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A condition that checks an inclusive interval normally combines two comparisons with AND. Using OR for x ≥ 1 or x ≤ 10 accepts every real x, because each value satisfies at least one comparison. Construct truth tables in a fixed order, then add intermediate columns for compound expressions. De Morgan’s relationships explain why NOT(A AND B) is equivalent to NOT A OR NOT B, while NOT(A OR B) is equivalent to NOT A AND NOT B. A loop condition must be interpreted with the construct: repeating until a condition is true differs from continuing while it is true.

topics.tip: NOT(A AND B) is not the same expression as NOT A AND NOT B.

worked.question: Evaluate (A AND NOT B) OR C for A = true, B = true, C = false.
steps: NOT B is false.
A AND NOT B is true AND false, which is false.
False OR C is false OR false, so the overall result is false.

False OR C is false OR false, so the overall result is false.

worked_examples.question: For Boolean inputs A and B, explain why NOT(A AND B) is not equivalent to NOT A AND NOT B.
steps: Take A = true and B = false.
A AND B is false, so NOT(A AND B) is true.
NOT A AND NOT B is false AND true, which is false; one differing case disproves equivalence.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Research, user needs and specifications

sections.heading: Start with an evidenced need
sections.body: A design problem describes the context and difficulty; a design brief states the intended task. Identify the user and the environment before proposing a solution. First-hand observation, interviews and product analysis reveal practical constraints. Secondary research adds material, technical and contextual knowledge. Record why each finding matters to a later design decision, rather than filling pages with unrelated images.

sections.heading: Turn findings into testable requirements
sections.body: A specification states what the product must achieve. Make criteria measurable where possible: dimensions, load, safe operation, cost, environmental exposure and maintenance. Distinguish essential constraints from preferences. Ergonomics concerns the relationship between people and products; anthropometric data supplies body measurements. Select relevant data ranges for the actual users and task, not simply an average person.

sections.heading: Generate and evaluate alternatives
sections.body: Produce genuinely different ideas before developing one. Use sketches, annotations and models to investigate mechanisms, construction and user interaction. Compare proposals against weighted or justified criteria; a decorative scoring table is weak without evidence. Show how feedback leads to changes. Good development explains why a decision improves function or manufacturability, not just that the new drawing looks better.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Research quality depends on relevance and interpretation. A photograph of an existing product becomes useful analysis when it identifies a feature, explains its effect and connects that finding to the design brief. Use more than one user or observation where practical to reduce dependence on one preference. A specification should distinguish a target from a testing method. A maximum dimension can be measured directly; comfort may require an appropriate user trial and a clearly described judgement. Keep the brief open enough to investigate alternatives before committing to a material, joint or mechanism.

topics.tip: A specification describes performance and constraints; it should not prematurely fix every construction detail.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Drawing, modelling, CAD and CAM

sections.heading: Communicate enough for someone else to understand
sections.body: Freehand sketches explore ideas quickly; annotations explain operation, materials and construction. Orthographic views communicate shape and dimensions, while pictorial views help a user visualise the object. Keep projection conventions consistent and include dimensions in suitable units. An exploded view can clarify assembly, and a sectional view can reveal hidden construction.

sections.heading: Models should answer a design question
sections.body: A card model can test proportion or access; a mechanism model can test movement. Full-size ergonomic mock-ups reveal reach and comfort problems that a small visual model may miss. Record the question, method, observation and design change. A polished model that tests nothing is less informative than a rough model with a clear purpose.

sections.heading: Digital tools change the workflow
sections.body: CAD can support accurate geometry, rapid revision and visualisation. CAM can improve repeatability when the toolpath, material, fixtures and machine settings are appropriate. Digital manufacture still needs process planning, tolerances, tool access and safety supervision. Account for cutter diameter, stock thickness or kerf rather than assuming the screen model is identical to the final part.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A manufacturing drawing should provide dimensions that remove ambiguity without unnecessary duplication. Orthographic views must align and use consistent projection conventions; hidden detail should not be confused with a visible edge. A prototype can be a test of function, scale, fit or user interaction, and need not reproduce every final material. When using CAM, a nominal digital dimension can produce a different physical fit because of kerf, tool diameter, stock variation and machine calibration. Test critical joints or slots on a small sample before committing all the final parts.

topics.tip: A rendered CAD image does not by itself prove that parts fit or can be manufactured.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Life cycles, production and responsible design

sections.heading: Look beyond the finished object
sections.body: A product life cycle includes extraction, processing, manufacture, transport, use and end of life. A lightweight product may still have high production impacts; a durable product may use more material but last longer. Design decisions need an explicit boundary and context. Repairability, replaceable components and accessible fastenings can extend useful life.

sections.heading: Choose a production scale that fits demand
sections.body: One-off production suits individual requirements but has high unit labour costs. Batch production makes groups with shared setup; mass production uses high volumes and specialised systems. Standard components reduce design effort and can simplify repair. Tolerances specify acceptable variation and should match functional need and process capability, rather than assuming all parts can be made perfectly exact.

sections.heading: Sustainability includes practical trade-offs
sections.body: Reduce unnecessary material, consider reuse and select realistic recycling routes. A recyclable material is not guaranteed to be recycled if collection or separation is impractical. Laminates, permanent adhesives and mixed materials can complicate end of life. Responsible evaluation also considers workers, users, accessibility, cost and cultural context. Justify a choice with product-specific evidence rather than calling a material universally eco-friendly.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A tolerance communicates an acceptable interval, not a demand for absolute precision. Use tighter tolerances where fit or safety requires them, while considering the capability and cost of the chosen process. Quality-control checks inspect whether outputs meet requirements; quality-assurance arrangements establish processes intended to make consistent quality more likely. Batch planning should consider setup, material flow and standard components. Sustainable choices require a lifecycle comparison: a product that uses more material initially may have lower total impact if it lasts longer, is maintained and replaces repeated disposable alternatives.

topics.tip: Evaluate the product life cycle; changing one material does not automatically reduce every environmental impact.

worked.question: Give two design changes that improve the repairability of a small wooden storage product.
steps: Use accessible mechanical fasteners where repeated disassembly is needed.
Use replaceable standard parts rather than permanently bonding every component.
Explain how these choices permit a damaged part to be replaced without destroying the whole product.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Structures, mechanisms and safe control

sections.heading: Forces affect shape and stability
sections.body: Products experience tension, compression, bending, torsion and shear. Triangulation can make a frame more rigid because a triangle resists shape change without altering side lengths. A wide support base and suitable centre of gravity improve stability. Reinforcement should address the actual load path; adding material indiscriminately may add weight without solving the weakness.

sections.heading: Mechanisms transform movement
sections.body: Levers trade force and displacement about a pivot. Gears transfer rotary motion and change speed, torque or direction; meshing gears rotate oppositely. Cams convert rotary input into a chosen follower motion, while linkages can change direction or coordinate movement. Consider guarding, wear, lubrication and the user’s access to moving parts when developing a mechanism.

sections.heading: Control needs inputs, processing and outputs
sections.body: A control system receives an input, processes a decision and operates an output. Feedback compares the actual state with a target and adjusts behaviour. When using electrical or mechanical systems in a school project, select components with suitable ratings and seek teacher approval for equipment, loads and power supplies. Risk controls belong in the plan and working practice, not only in a final written list.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A design’s load path follows how forces pass through parts and joints into the supports. Reinforcing a surface far from the critical joint may not prevent the actual failure. Gears trade speed and torque according to their tooth ratio, while friction and other losses mean a real output does not receive all the input power. For feedback control, identify the measured variable, target, comparison and corrective output. A sensor alone is not a complete control system. Guarding should account for foreseeable user contact with pinch points and moving parts, alongside workshop operating instructions.

topics.tip: Mechanical advantage is not free energy: reducing effort force usually increases the distance moved.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Project portfolio, manufacture and evaluation

sections.heading: The project records a developing argument
sections.body: For the 2027 course, the project contributes half of the qualification alongside two written components. A strong portfolio connects the identified need, research, specification, alternative ideas, development, production planning and evaluation. Keep evidence selective and legible. Your centre’s instructions, assessment criteria and authenticated work requirements govern the actual submission; revision notes do not replace teacher guidance.

sections.heading: Plan manufacturing before irreversible steps
sections.body: An ordered production plan identifies material preparation, marking, shaping, joining, assembly, finishing and checks. Include dimensions, tolerances, tools, fixtures and suitable safety controls. Record changes honestly when the process differs from the plan and explain the reason. Test critical interfaces early; discovering a fit problem before finishing is easier to correct than after final assembly.

sections.heading: Evaluate against the original requirements
sections.body: Test the product using methods appropriate to its intended use and safe school practice. Combine measured performance with relevant user feedback. Explain what met the specification, what did not and why. Propose specific realistic improvements and consider their consequences. A neat product with no meaningful testing is not fully evaluated; a thoughtful evaluation can identify limitations without pretending the design has none.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: An effective project record forms a chain of justified decisions. A finding from research should influence a specification point, idea or test; a failed model should lead to an explained development; a manufacturing change should be recorded with its reason. Separate evidence collected during the process from a reflection written afterwards. Evaluation should return to the original measurable criteria and include relevant user evidence, not only personal satisfaction. Proposed improvements should be sufficiently specific to test and should consider consequences for cost, construction and appearance. Follow the centre’s current authenticated-work requirements throughout.

topics.tip: Keep project work your own. Use Rian AI for explanations and feedback, not fabricated research or evidence.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Timbers and manufactured boards

sections.heading: Material families are starting points, not quality grades
sections.body: Hardwoods come from broad-leaved trees and softwoods from conifers; the names do not guarantee physical hardness. Timber is anisotropic: properties depend on grain direction. Knots, splits and moisture content influence strength and working behaviour. Seasoning reduces moisture to improve stability, but timber can still absorb or lose moisture in use.

sections.heading: Boards offer different compromises
sections.body: Plywood uses bonded veneers with alternating grain directions, giving useful dimensional stability. MDF has a uniform fibre structure and machines well but creates fine dust and needs suitable extraction. Chipboard is economical but edge strength and moisture resistance depend on grade. Veneers can improve appearance while using a different core material. Specify an appropriate board grade for wet or demanding environments.

sections.heading: Match property, process and product
sections.body: Choose timber for load, appearance, exposure, availability, cost and workability. Orient grain and position joints to support the expected forces. Plan how movement might affect panels and fastenings. Use finishes to protect or enhance surfaces, but do not treat a coating as a substitute for suitable material selection. Responsible sourcing matters alongside efficient cutting layouts and reduced waste.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Solid wood movement is greatest across rather than along the grain, so wide panels may require construction that accommodates moisture-related dimensional change. Manufactured boards can reduce some variability but do not all behave alike. Plywood’s alternating veneers distribute grain directions; MDF offers a uniform machining surface but needs suitable dust control; chipboard performance depends on particle bonding and grade. Identify visible faces, exposed edges, fixing positions and expected moisture exposure before choosing a board. A decorative veneer changes the surface appearance but does not automatically change the core’s structural or moisture behaviour.

topics.tip: Hardwood does not always mean physically harder than every softwood.

worked.question: Explain why plywood may suit a portable carrying case better than a wide thin solid-wood panel.
steps: Alternating veneer directions improve dimensional stability compared with movement across a wide solid panel.
It can provide useful strength with relatively thin sections and good panel dimensions.
The actual choice must still account for plywood grade, edges, moisture exposure and joining.

cards.answer: controlled reduction of timber moisture content

cards.answer: a thin sheet of wood used in a layered or surface construction

cards.question: Explain why a joint design for a wide solid-wood panel may need to accommodate movement.
cards.answer: Wood can absorb or lose moisture as environmental conditions change. Its dimensions change more across the grain than along it. A completely restrictive fixing arrangement can cause distortion or splitting, so a suitable construction permits controlled movement.

cards.answer: Softwood and hardwood are botanical classifications. They do not guarantee an ordering of hardness, durability or price for every species.

topics.subject: Design & Technology

sections.heading: Properties should be linked to the failure you want to avoid
sections.body: Strength concerns resistance to failure under load; stiffness concerns resistance to elastic deformation. Toughness concerns energy absorbed before fracture, and hardness concerns resistance to indentation or scratching. Ductility allows drawing into wire and malleability allows forming into sheet. A material can be hard yet brittle, so do not use strong, tough and hard as synonyms.

sections.heading: Metals and alloys provide specialised combinations
sections.body: Ferrous metals contain iron; corrosion behaviour depends on composition and treatment. Low-carbon steel can be readily formed and welded, stainless steels offer useful corrosion resistance, and aluminium alloys can provide low density. Copper is valued for electrical and thermal conductivity. Selection must balance required properties, manufacturing processes, cost, section form and environmental exposure.

sections.heading: Polymers respond differently to heat
sections.body: Thermoplastics can soften and be reshaped on heating within suitable processing limits. Thermosetting polymers form networks that do not remelt in the same way; overheating can degrade them. Additives and reinforcement modify properties. Acrylic may provide clarity but can crack under poor machining or stress; polypropylene is useful for some repeated-flexure applications. Identify the precise grade and process rather than relying only on the material family.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Choose a property by considering the failure mode. A cover may need impact toughness rather than just scratch hardness; a shelf may need stiffness as well as strength. Section shape and thickness influence performance alongside material. Thermoplastic and thermosetting describe response to heat and molecular structure, not whether a product is generally strong. A polymer grade can contain fillers or reinforcement that changes behaviour. For metal selection, corrosion resistance, finish, forming, joining and cost must be considered together, because a suitable base material can still fail through an unsuitable joint or surface treatment.

topics.tip: Stiffness and strength answer different questions: bending less is not the same as resisting fracture.

sections.heading: Accuracy begins with a datum
sections.body: A datum is a reference surface, edge or line from which other measurements are made. Establish square, flat references before marking. Use an appropriate rule, square, marking gauge or measuring instrument for the required tolerance. Mark waste and identify paired parts. Repeatedly measuring from previously cut edges can accumulate error; reference critical dimensions consistently.

sections.heading: Select a process for the material and shape
sections.body: Sawing removes stock along a planned cut, drilling makes holes, filing refines edges and suitable machining produces controlled forms. Account for the saw kerf and finish to the line where needed. For a hole, centre marking and secure workholding improve positioning. Tool choice, speed and feed depend on the material, tool and school equipment guidance.

sections.heading: Make quality control part of the sequence
sections.body: Check dimensions, squareness, fit and surface condition at stages where correction is still possible. Use jigs for repeatable positioning and fixtures for secure support, distinguishing their roles where required. Keep guards, extraction and appropriate protective equipment in use. Never hold a workpiece by hand for a machine operation that requires clamping, and follow trained supervision rather than improvising a technique from notes.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A process plan needs a datum strategy as well as nominal dimensions. Mark critical features from a consistent reference and check the reference remains square and undamaged. Tool geometry affects the final shape: an internal milled corner cannot be sharper than the cutter permits without another operation. A jig can guide repeatable tool positioning, while a fixture securely locates or holds the work. Measure at points where an error can still be corrected. Workshop safety depends on trained supervision, correct guarding and secure workholding, not merely a list of protective clothing in the portfolio.

topics.tip: Check the actual material thickness before designing slots or finger joints.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Joints, adhesives, fasteners and assembly

sections.heading: A joint must suit its forces and construction
sections.body: Butt joints are simple but may need reinforcement; housings locate shelves; mortise-and-tenon arrangements provide useful frame connections. Dowel and finger joints offer other positioning or glue-area advantages. The best joint depends on section size, grain, load direction, access, equipment and whether disassembly is needed. A named joint without a contextual reason is only a partial justification.

sections.heading: Permanent and removable connections differ
sections.body: Screws, bolts and suitable fittings permit some disassembly; adhesives can produce continuous bonded areas but may complicate repair. Choose adhesive for both materials, service conditions, surface preparation and cure requirements. Clamp correctly without forcing parts out of alignment. Metal joining includes mechanical fastening, soldering, brazing and welding, each with different operating temperatures, joint properties and safety requirements.

sections.heading: Assembly order can determine whether a design is possible
sections.body: Trial-fit critical parts before final bonding or finishing. Check squareness, clearances and fastener access. Consider which surfaces will become inaccessible and whether a component must be inserted before closing an assembly. Allow for material movement and use appropriate pilot or clearance holes. A production drawing should communicate the joint detail and required fit, not leave the manufacturer to guess.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A joint may carry tension, shear, bending or a combination, and its shape and fastenings should address those loads. Adhesive joints require compatible materials, suitable surface preparation, the correct bond-line conditions and adequate cure. A large bonded area can help, but poor fit or contamination can still make it fail. Removable fasteners need access for assembly and later maintenance. Plan the assembly sequence so a tool can reach each fixing and a captured component is inserted before its enclosure is closed. A successful trial fit should be checked before applying a finish that changes clearances.

topics.tip: Adhesive performance depends strongly on preparation and curing; more adhesive is not automatically a stronger joint.

topics.title: Forming, casting, heat treatment and finishes

sections.heading: Shape can be added, removed or transformed
sections.body: Subtractive processes remove material; forming changes shape; casting introduces material into a mould. Thermoplastic sheet can be heated and formed within a safe controlled process. Metal sheet may be bent around suitable tooling. Casting needs allowance for material flow, shrinkage and removal. The appropriate process depends on quantity, shape complexity, material and available equipment.

sections.heading: Treatment changes the working behaviour
sections.body: Annealing can soften suitable metals and reduce effects of prior working; hardening and tempering can modify suitable steels. The process and outcome depend on composition, heating, cooling and supervision. Do not assume every metal responds identically. A school revision explanation describes the principle; it is not a safe procedure for unsupervised furnaces, molten material or chemical treatment.

sections.heading: A finish protects as well as communicates quality
sections.body: Paint, varnish, oil, wax, plating and other treatments have different appearance, wear and maintenance properties. Prepare the substrate, remove defects and ensure compatibility between layers. Some finishes protect against corrosion or moisture while others mainly enhance appearance. Plan masking and inaccessible surfaces. Specify ventilation, drying and disposal according to the product instructions and workshop rules.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: Casting design must permit the pattern or finished part to be removed from its mould, allowing for geometry, shrinkage and the chosen mould system. A forming process changes shape without the same material removal as machining, but can introduce springback or thinning. Heat-treatment effects depend on composition and the complete heating-and-cooling process; applying a term such as annealing without naming the material and intended property is incomplete. Surface finishing can improve protection and appearance but needs preparation, compatible layers and appropriate drying or curing. Follow product instructions and school procedures for ventilation, heat and chemical handling.

topics.tip: A finish cannot reliably repair a poorly fitting joint or an unsuitable base material.

topics.title: Structures, motion and electronic control

sections.heading: Choose the option deliberately
sections.body: Systems & Control is an alternative 2027 specialist route, not an additional compulsory paper for the Resistant Materials route. Structures carry loads through frames and members, while mechanisms transmit motion. Identify compression and tension in members and explain how triangulation, section shape or reinforcement influences stiffness and load capacity.

sections.heading: Mechanisms trade speed, direction and force
sections.body: A gear train’s tooth counts determine its speed ratio. Belts, pulleys, chains and sprockets offer different alignment and slip properties. Cams and linkages convert motion patterns. Bearings reduce friction and support moving shafts. Explain a mechanism using its input, output and intermediate interactions; saying it makes the product work does not establish its suitability.

sections.heading: Electronic systems connect sensing to response
sections.body: An input such as a light or temperature sensor changes an electrical signal. A processing stage compares, switches or amplifies, and an output such as a lamp, motor or buzzer responds. Use component ratings, suitable power supplies and protection. Feedback can maintain a controlled condition. Circuit and mechanical tests should use approved school equipment and teacher-guided methods.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A gear train’s ratio depends on the driver and driven tooth counts, while an idler changes direction or spacing without changing the overall simple ratio between the first and last gears. A belt drive may slip under load, which can be either a limitation or a protective effect in a suitable design. A feedback diagram should separate sensor, comparison and output stages. Real electronic outputs may need a driver stage because a sensor or logic output cannot directly supply a motor’s current. Select safe low-voltage components and ratings using approved school guidance.

sections.heading: Draw the information the reader needs
sections.body: Graphic Products is another 2027 specialist route. Orthographic drawings communicate separate aligned views, while isometric and perspective views help visualise form. Add dimensions, line conventions and annotations appropriately. Construction accuracy and clarity matter more than decorative shading when the question asks for a technical view.

sections.heading: Flat developments need working allowances
sections.body: A development unfolds a three-dimensional surface into a two-dimensional pattern. Packaging nets need tabs, closures, folds and allowances for actual material thickness. Grain direction, scoring and bending influence performance. Test a model to check that faces meet and that a user can open, close and carry the package without damaging it.

sections.heading: Presentation and manufacture use material constraints
sections.body: Typography, contrast, hierarchy and layout make information readable. Paper, card, boards and suitable polymers have differing stiffness, surface and forming properties. Printing, cutting, folding, joining and finishing must fit the quantity and use. CAD and CAM can improve repeatability, but the designer still needs to account for registration, tool geometry, tolerances and disposal or recycling routes.

sections.heading: Reason it through
sections.body: A packaging development should show fold and cut lines distinctly and include tabs or other closures that can actually be assembled. Material thickness changes how adjacent faces meet, while grain direction and scoring influence fold quality. For a technical drawing, choose line conventions and views for construction information; for communication graphics, use contrast and hierarchy so the intended message remains legible at the final size. topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Immunity, antibodies and vaccination

sections.heading: Three complementary defences
sections.body: Physical barriers reduce entry of pathogens. Skin forms a protective barrier, mucus can trap particles, and cilia help move contaminated mucus away from parts of the respiratory tract. If a pathogen enters tissues, white blood cells contribute to defence. Phagocytes can engulf and digest microorganisms. Lymphocytes participate in more specific responses, including antibody production and the formation of immune memory. These roles should be distinguished rather than attributing every process to every white blood cell.

sections.heading: Specific recognition and memory
sections.body: Antigens are molecular features recognised by the immune system. An antibody has a binding region complementary to a particular antigenic feature. Following recognition, suitable lymphocyte populations multiply, producing a targeted response. Some cells persist as memory cells. On a later exposure to the same relevant antigen, a faster and larger response may control the pathogen before serious disease develops. Specificity explains why immunity to one infection does not imply equal protection against every other infection.

sections.heading: Interpreting vaccination evidence
sections.body: Vaccination introduces a preparation that safely stimulates a response to relevant antigens without the same risk as the disease itself. The form of the preparation varies. A primary response develops over time; later doses can strengthen immune memory. In a graph, compare delay, peak response and duration, and link those observations to memory rather than simply labelling the second curve better. Population-level protection depends on the pathogen, vaccine effectiveness and participation; it is not an absolute guarantee for every individual.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: The eye, reflexes and accommodation

sections.heading: Light detection and protection
sections.body: Light enters through the cornea and pupil, passes through the lens and reaches the retina. The iris changes pupil diameter, controlling how much light enters. The retina contains light-sensitive cells; the optic nerve carries resulting information towards the brain. The sclera provides a tough outer layer and the choroid supports the retina and reduces internal reflection. Name the structure first, then connect its property to its function.

sections.heading: Focusing at different distances
sections.body: Accommodation changes lens shape. For a near object, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments become less taut, and the lens becomes thicker and more strongly converging. For a distant object, ciliary muscles relax, ligaments become taut, and the lens becomes thinner. The cornea provides substantial refraction, but normal accommodation primarily changes the lens. The objective is to focus the image at the retina rather than move the retina towards the focus.

sections.heading: Two responses with different purposes
sections.body: The pupil reflex responds to light level, whereas accommodation responds to focusing demand. In bright light, the pupil becomes smaller, reducing incoming light. A reflex pathway can protect tissues without a conscious decision. Distinguish stimulus, receptor, coordinator and effector in the response. Do not claim that increasing the pupil size automatically brings a blurred near image into focus; that confuses light regulation with changing the optical power of the lens.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Hormonal control of the menstrual cycle

sections.heading: Coordinate the ovary and uterus
sections.body: The menstrual cycle involves related changes in the ovary and uterine lining. FSH supports follicle development and stimulates oestrogen secretion. Rising oestrogen supports rebuilding of the uterine lining and participates in feedback on pituitary hormone release. A suitable hormonal pattern leads to a surge of LH, which triggers ovulation. These are coordinated processes, so a complete explanation links a hormone to its target and effect.

sections.heading: After ovulation
sections.body: The remains of the follicle form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. Progesterone helps maintain the uterine lining and inhibits further FSH and LH release. If pregnancy is not established, hormone levels fall as the corpus luteum declines, and the lining is shed. If pregnancy is established, other hormonal signals maintain support. A simplified school cycle diagram illustrates relationships, but actual cycle lengths and timings vary.

sections.heading: Read a graph rather than memorising one date
sections.body: Use the plotted hormone pattern and the question’s time scale to identify events. A sharp LH peak is associated with ovulation; a later progesterone rise relates to the corpus luteum. Different graphs may use different scales for different hormones, so apparent line heights cannot always be compared as absolute concentrations. State the hormone, its source where required, its effect and the relevant feedback link.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: DNA to protein: transcription and translation

sections.heading: The code is a sequence
sections.body: DNA consists of two strands with complementary base pairing. The sequence along a strand carries information; the fact that a molecule contains four kinds of base is not sufficient to specify a protein. A gene contains information related to a functional product. In protein-coding contexts, the order of bases determines a sequence of amino acids through an RNA intermediate. An amino-acid chain must fold appropriately to perform its biological role.

sections.heading: Transcription and translation are different stages
sections.body: During transcription, an RNA copy is made from a DNA template. RNA contains uracil rather than thymine in the usual school comparison. During translation, a ribosome reads the messenger-RNA sequence in codons, and transfer RNA helps deliver corresponding amino acids. The growing chain follows the codon sequence. Do not describe the DNA molecule as leaving the nucleus and travelling to every ribosome as part of this normal eukaryotic process.

sections.heading: Relate mutation to function carefully
sections.body: A base change can alter a codon, which may alter an amino acid and protein structure. This can affect an active site or another functional region. However, some changes produce no amino-acid change, and some amino-acid changes have little detectable effect. A causal explanation should avoid claiming every mutation is harmful or every mutation must change a protein. Use the exact sequence or evidence supplied in the problem.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Carbon and nitrogen cycles

sections.heading: Follow atoms through transformations
sections.body: Photosynthesis takes carbon from carbon dioxide into organic molecules. Feeding transfers these molecules between organisms, while respiration releases carbon dioxide. Decomposers use organic material from dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon through respiration. Combustion releases carbon from fuels or biomass. Carbon is transferred and chemically rearranged; energy entering the ecosystem is not recycled by exactly the same processes.

sections.heading: Nitrogen becomes usable through microorganisms
sections.body: Atmospheric nitrogen is not directly usable by most plants. Nitrogen fixation converts it into compounds that can enter biological systems. Decomposition releases ammonium compounds from organic nitrogen. Nitrifying microorganisms oxidise ammonium through nitrite to nitrate under suitable aerobic conditions. Plants absorb mineral nitrogen and use it in molecules such as amino acids. Denitrifying microorganisms can return nitrogen to the atmosphere, particularly where oxygen is limited.

sections.heading: Connect the cycle to farming and pollution
sections.body: Harvest removes nitrogen-containing material from an area, so nutrient replacement may be needed to sustain production. Excess fertiliser can enter waterways and contribute to eutrophication. Waterlogged soils can favour nitrogen losses through denitrification. When asked about bacteria, identify the process and chemical direction rather than saying all bacteria make nitrates. Biological cycles describe interacting populations and environmental conditions, not one universal linear chain.
