topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Sampling, biodiversity and ecological data

sections.heading: Match sampling to the question
sections.body: Use quadrats for organisms that can be sampled in a fixed area and a transect to investigate change along a gradient. Random coordinates reduce selection of unusually convenient or impressive locations. Repeated quadrats provide a mean and some information about variability. Systematic positions along a transect can reveal a relationship with distance, but they answer a different question from a random area survey.

sections.heading: Calculate with the sampled area
sections.body: Density is number counted divided by total area sampled. Multiply a representative density by habitat area to estimate abundance. Percentage cover can be more useful than counting individual plants when boundaries between individuals are unclear. Compare results using equal effort or an appropriate adjustment. Species richness is a count of species; biodiversity can also involve how evenly individuals are distributed among those species.

sections.heading: Evaluate the conclusion
sections.body: A correlation between light intensity and a species’ abundance does not isolate light as the cause: soil moisture or disturbance may vary too. Explain how variables are measured, consider replication and identify realistic limitations. Sampling may miss seasonal or mobile organisms. Give an estimate with a justified degree of confidence rather than claiming a quadrat survey measures every organism in the entire ecosystem directly.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Food tests and enzyme investigations

sections.heading: Separate the tests and observations
sections.body: Iodine changes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present. Benedict’s reagent is used with a suitable heated-water-bath method to test for reducing sugars, producing a coloured precipitate when positive. The Biuret test gives a purple or lilac colour with protein. An ethanol emulsion method gives a cloudy white emulsion with lipid. Use the reagents and safety instructions supplied by the school; ethanol is flammable and should not be heated over a flame.

sections.heading: Control the enzyme reaction
sections.body: An enzyme experiment changes one independent variable while measuring a defined response. For amylase and starch, repeated sampling into iodine can identify when starch is no longer detected. Keep reagent quantities, mixing, sampling interval and other conditions consistent. A pH investigation needs suitable buffers; a temperature investigation needs time for reagents to reach the intended temperature. Use repeat trials to check consistency.

sections.heading: Interpret a time endpoint
sections.body: For a fixed amount of substrate, shorter completion time usually indicates a faster rate under comparable conditions. Reciprocal time can provide a comparative rate measure. It does not mean every enzyme reaction has exactly that rate law. An endpoint has uncertainty because the change may occur between samples. Denaturation explains loss of function at sufficiently high temperature, whereas lower temperature normally reduces rate without permanently changing the active site.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.title: Nephrons, water balance and ADH

sections.heading: Filtration is selective by size
sections.body: Blood pressure drives small molecules from the glomerular blood into the kidney capsule. Water, ions, glucose and urea can enter the filtrate, while blood cells and large proteins are normally retained. This initial filtering does not identify which substances the body should discard. The composition must be modified further as the filtrate passes through the nephron.

sections.heading: Useful substances are recovered
sections.body: Selective reabsorption transfers useful substances back into the blood. Glucose is normally recovered, along with needed water and ions. Different nephron regions contribute to concentration and regulation. Final urine therefore differs from the initial filtrate. Urea derives from amino-acid metabolism in the liver and is removed through the kidneys; naming the place of excretion is not the same as naming where the waste was formed.

sections.heading: ADH coordinates a water-saving response
sections.body: When blood water potential falls, the coordinating system increases ADH release. ADH increases water permeability of the collecting ducts, allowing more water to be reabsorbed under the appropriate gradients. The resulting urine volume is lower and more concentrated. When more water is available, lower ADH reduces this water-saving effect. Explain the response as negative feedback with a detected change, hormone action and an outcome that opposes the original deviation.

a hormone regulating collecting-duct water permeability

worked.question: Compare the expected urine volume and concentration after a large water intake with those during dehydration.
steps: After a large water intake, ADH is lower and less water is reabsorbed through this mechanism.
Urine is therefore generally larger in volume and more dilute.
During dehydration, higher ADH promotes water recovery, producing less, more concentrated urine.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae

sections.heading: Mass ratios are not atom ratios
sections.body: A formula records relative numbers of atoms. Start from masses or percentage composition and divide each element’s mass by its relative atomic mass. The resulting mole values are proportional to atom numbers. Dividing by the smallest value gives a ratio that may need multiplying to remove simple fractions. Do not round a ratio near 1.5 directly to 2; check whether multiplying all parts by two gives a sensible whole-number ratio.

sections.heading: From empirical to molecular information
sections.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio. A molecular formula gives the actual atom numbers in a molecule. Divide the molecular relative mass by the empirical-formula mass to obtain an integer multiplier, then multiply every subscript. Ionic giant structures are described by their formula ratio rather than a molecular formula for an isolated molecule in the same way.

sections.heading: Interpret an experiment critically
sections.body: A metal-oxide experiment can use the change in mass as oxygen gained, under the stated assumptions. Loss of product, incomplete oxidation or reaction with another gas can affect the inferred composition. State which mass is measured directly and which is found by subtraction. Repeating a heating-and-weighing cycle to constant mass can support completion, but does not prove every other experimental assumption is correct.

key_terms.definition: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound
the actual numbers of atoms in a molecule
a stable measured mass after repeated specified treatment and weighing

worked.question: A compound contains 24 g carbon and 6 g hydrogen. Find its empirical formula using Aᵣ(C)=12 and Aᵣ(H)=1.
steps: Moles of carbon = 24/12 = 2; moles of hydrogen = 6/1 = 6.
The ratio 2:6 simplifies to 1:3.
The empirical formula is CH₃.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Titration calculations and soluble salts

sections.heading: Use the reacting ratio
sections.body: A titration combines measured volumes with a balanced chemical equation. Convert volumes to dm³ when using mol dm⁻³. Calculate the moles in the known solution, use the equation’s coefficient ratio, then find the concentration of the unknown. An acid-base reaction is not always a 1:1 mole relationship; sulfuric acid reacting fully with sodium hydroxide is a useful counterexample.

sections.heading: Make the measured volume reliable
sections.body: An initial rough titration locates the approximate endpoint. Later trials approach it carefully with mixing and dropwise addition near the change. Use suitable concordant titres according to the question or laboratory guidance. Read the burette consistently and calculate delivered volume from the difference between readings. Rinse apparatus appropriately so unwanted water or residues do not alter the effective concentrations.

sections.heading: Prepare a salt without indicator contamination
sections.body: When both acid and base are soluble, adding an excess leaves contamination that cannot simply be filtered away. A titration establishes the required amounts. A preparation can then use measured quantities without indicator before concentration and crystallisation. The actual method and indicator depend on the chemicals and school instructions. In evaluation, identify a specific source of error and explain the direction of its effect where possible.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Ion tests and evidence from observations

sections.heading: Test a clear hypothesis
sections.body: Analytical tests identify evidence for particular ions under stated conditions. Flame tests can identify selected metal ions, such as sodium’s yellow or copper’s characteristic blue-green flame. Avoid transferring contamination between samples. Sodium hydroxide can form coloured metal hydroxide precipitates, while some white precipitates dissolve in excess reagent. State the observation before inferring the ion.

sections.heading: Use suitable reagents for negative ions
sections.body: A halide test commonly uses nitric acid followed by silver nitrate: chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide cream and iodide yellow. A sulfate test uses an appropriate acidified barium reagent to form white barium sulfate. Carbonates release carbon dioxide with a suitable acid; identify that gas using limewater. The exact acid matters because it must not introduce the ion being tested or create a misleading precipitate.

sections.heading: A test result has conditions and limits
sections.body: The presence of one ion may interfere with a test for another, so sequence and acidification are part of the method. A negative result could reflect low concentration or an unsuitable procedure as well as genuine absence. Use the specification’s required ions and the method supplied in an exam. Handle reagents under school supervision; these notes explain observations rather than authorise unsupervised chemical testing.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Calorimetry and uncertainty in energy measurements

sections.heading: Define the system and the measured change
sections.body: A simple reaction calorimeter commonly measures the temperature change of a solution. Approximate heat transferred using q = mcΔT, stating assumptions about density, heat capacity and heat losses. The solution gaining heat corresponds to the reaction transferring energy out. A positive solution temperature rise therefore does not mean the reaction’s enthalpy change is positive.

sections.heading: Scale to a stated amount of reaction
sections.body: Use moles of the appropriate limiting reactant and the equation’s reaction basis when calculating a molar energy change. Convert joules to kilojoules consistently. An approximate water heat capacity must not be mixed with an incompatible mass unit. For combustion, heat absorbed by water is only a portion of the fuel’s total transferred energy in a simple open experiment.

sections.heading: Explain realistic limitations
sections.body: Heat escaping to the surroundings, energy absorbed by the container, incomplete combustion and evaporation can each influence the result. Name the mechanism and explain its likely effect rather than saying human error. Insulation and a lid can reduce some losses but introduce their own practical considerations. Repeat measurements estimate consistency; they do not automatically correct a systematic error present in every trial.

The reaction transfers energy out, so the estimate is −42 kJ mol⁻¹.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Designing rate experiments and reading curves

sections.heading: Choose a measurable change
sections.body: A reaction rate can be investigated by gas volume, loss of mass or time to a specified visual change. Each method measures a particular consequence of reaction and has different limitations. A gas syringe can measure accumulated gas, but leaks and delayed connection reduce the measured amount. A balance measures mass lost when gas escapes, so its interpretation depends on which species leave and whether evaporation also occurs.

sections.heading: Control the comparison
sections.body: For a concentration investigation, keep relevant quantities such as reactant form, temperature and total liquid volume appropriately controlled. For surface area, use the same reactant mass while changing particle size. Record sufficient points to show the early steep region and later plateau. Compare initial gradients to investigate rate, while final gas volumes reflect reacting amounts and limiting reagents rather than rate alone.

sections.heading: Use gradients with units
sections.body: Mean rate is change in measured quantity divided by time interval. Instantaneous rate uses a tangent to a curve at the stated time. Draw a sufficiently large gradient triangle and read both axes carefully. For time-to-endpoint methods, reciprocal time can compare runs with the same endpoint. A catalyst can make completion earlier without changing the theoretical final product amount from fixed starting quantities.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Naming structures, isomers and ester formation

sections.heading: A formula must show the intended connectivity
sections.body: A molecular formula gives atom counts but not a unique arrangement. Structural and displayed formulae communicate how atoms connect. Check carbon’s usual valency of four, oxygen’s of two and hydrogen’s of one in the neutral compounds studied. A branch can change the name and physical behaviour without changing the molecular formula. Different drawings can also represent the same connectivity after rotation, so compare bonds rather than the page orientation.

sections.heading: Use the functional group in the name
sections.body: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid can form an ester and water under suitable catalysed conditions. The alcohol gives the ester’s alkyl part; the acid gives its carboxylate part. Methanol and ethanoic acid therefore produce methyl ethanoate. The functional group determines much of the chemistry, while carbon-chain length also influences physical properties. The OH within a carboxyl group is not a separate free hydroxide ion.

sections.heading: Link representation to polymerisation
sections.body: In addition polymerisation, open the alkene double bond to show connections to neighbouring repeat units and retain side groups. Include continuation bonds through brackets. In condensation polymerisation, show the relevant linking groups and identify the small molecule eliminated in the stated reaction. A formula exercise assesses atom conservation as well as recognition of a reaction name.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Investigating current-voltage characteristics

sections.heading: Build the measurement circuit
sections.body: Use an ammeter in series with the component and a voltmeter across it. A suitable variable supply or resistance controls the operating point. Take paired voltage and current readings and record the direction of each quantity consistently. Reverse polarity where the approved circuit and component permit it to investigate the other branch. Protect the component from excessive current and follow the school’s circuit instructions.

sections.heading: Recognise the shapes
sections.body: An ohmic resistor at constant temperature gives a straight current-voltage graph through the origin. A filament lamp’s curve becomes less steep as it heats and resistance increases, when current is plotted vertically against voltage. A diode shows strong directional behaviour, with relatively little current in reverse under the normal intended operating conditions. Axis choice matters when interpreting steepness.

sections.heading: Separate component behaviour from experimental effects
sections.body: Heating is the intended reason for the lamp’s changing resistance, but can be an unwanted confound in a resistor investigation. Allow suitable cooling or limit current where needed. Calculate V/I at a point to obtain that operating resistance; do not automatically call the tangent gradient resistance on every graph. Check instrument ranges, connections and zero readings before attributing an unexpected curve to new physics.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Measuring motion and evaluating timing

sections.heading: Define the measured interval
sections.body: Average speed uses distance travelled during a measured interval. In a light-gate experiment, a known interrupting flag length and blockage time can estimate the object’s speed at the gate. Between two gates, use their separation and the travel time for average speed over that region. These are different intervals and must not be confused. A video method needs a distance scale and known frame interval.

sections.heading: Calculate and compare acceleration
sections.body: Estimate acceleration from a change in measured velocity divided by elapsed time. For motion on a slope, identify forces and the intended control variables. A constant average acceleration over one interval does not prove the acceleration is unchanged at every instant. Repeated trials can reveal variability, while calibration of length and timing affects systematic accuracy.

sections.heading: Judge improvements specifically
sections.body: Reducing human reaction-time effects can be useful for short intervals, but an automatic instrument still needs correct setup. An incorrectly measured flag length biases every speed calculated from it. Increasing travel distance can make manual timing relatively less sensitive to a fixed timing uncertainty, provided the motion remains appropriate for the model. Record units and keep enough significant figures during intermediate calculations.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Thermal measurements and gas-law calculations

sections.heading: Choose the correct thermal model
sections.body: A temperature rise uses E = mcΔT. A change of state uses E = mL for the stated latent heat. If both occur, calculate separate stages and add their energy transfers rather than applying one equation to the entire process. Real experiments may also warm the container or lose energy to the surroundings. State assumptions before interpreting a result as a material constant.

sections.heading: Keep gas conditions explicit
sections.body: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pV is constant in the simple model. If volume is fixed, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. Convert Celsius to kelvin when using temperature ratios. A change from 20°C to 40°C is not a doubling of absolute temperature. The measured pressure should be the appropriate absolute pressure when the relationship requires it.

sections.heading: Explain behaviour using particles
sections.body: Compressing a gas at constant temperature increases collision frequency with the container walls, raising pressure. Heating at constant volume increases mean particle kinetic energy and collision effects. A particle explanation should connect motion, collision and force per area rather than say particles become bigger. During a phase change, energy changes separation or arrangement instead of the same increase in mean kinetic energy as a temperature rise.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Background radiation and decay calculations

sections.heading: A detector does not measure only the source
sections.body: Count rates include background radiation from the surroundings and detector conditions. Measure background for a suitable interval and use a corresponding rate. Subtract it from source-plus-background readings before analysing the source’s change. Keep detector geometry and measurement procedure consistent. Random variation means successive short measurements will not usually match exactly even when source activity is effectively constant.

sections.heading: Apply half-life to the corrected quantity
sections.body: After each half-life, activity or undecayed-nucleus count is halved. Work through repeated halvings or use a power of one half. A measured total count rate eventually approaches background rather than zero. If the question asks for the final detector reading, add background back after calculating the remaining source contribution. A half-life is not the time for every nucleus to decay.

sections.heading: Interpret graphs and uncertainty
sections.body: Read several suitable half-life intervals rather than selecting a single noisy pair where possible. Longer counting intervals collect more events and can reduce relative statistical variation, but the source may itself change appreciably during the interval. Distinguish activity in becquerels from a detector’s counts per second; detection efficiency and geometry mean they are not automatically equal.

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Set notation and Venn-diagram reasoning

sections.heading: Describe membership precisely
sections.body: A set is a collection of specified objects or values. The universal set defines everything under consideration. A complement contains members of the universal set outside a named set. The intersection contains common members, while the union includes members of either set, counting the overlap once. A Venn diagram should represent the stated universal set, not an assumed unlimited collection.

sections.heading: Fill overlapping regions in a useful order
sections.body: Place the most specific overlap first, then subtract it from the given set totals to fill exclusive regions. Complete the outside region using the universal total. For three sets, distinguish a pairwise intersection that includes the central triple region from an exclusive two-set region. Check that the separate diagram regions add to the universal total.

sections.heading: Turn a region into a probability

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.title: Quadratic inequalities and solution regions

sections.heading: Roots divide the number line
sections.body: For a quadratic inequality, first find the roots of the corresponding equality. They divide the real number line into intervals within which a continuous quadratic’s sign is fixed. A factorised expression helps determine the sign by considering each factor. Include a root when equality is permitted and exclude it for a strict inequality.

sections.heading: Use sign or graph evidence
sections.body: For an upward-opening quadratic with two distinct real roots, the graph is negative between the roots and positive outside. A downward-opening quadratic reverses that pattern. If the expression is multiplied or divided by a negative number during rearrangement, reverse the inequality sign. A test value from each interval provides a useful check and is safer than memorising between the roots as a universal rule.

sections.heading: Intersect simultaneous restrictions
sections.body: If a solution must satisfy several inequalities, take the intersection of their allowed regions. For integer solutions, identify which integers lie inside the final intervals and handle strict endpoints correctly. In coordinate problems, boundaries can be lines or curves and the feasible region consists of points satisfying every condition. State a union of separate intervals clearly when the permitted values are outside two roots.

topics.title: Differentiation and optimisation models

sections.heading: Model the quantity before differentiating
sections.body: Define the variable and the physical or mathematical domain. Use the stated constraint to express the quantity being optimised in terms of one variable. Differentiation then identifies how that quantity changes. A stationary value is a candidate, not a complete answer until the domain and maximum-or-minimum condition have been considered.

sections.heading: Apply polynomial differentiation
sections.body: For polynomial terms, multiply by the power and reduce the power by one. Constants differentiate to zero. Set the derivative equal to zero to find stationary input values, then substitute into the original quantity to find the corresponding output. Check a change of derivative sign, the graph shape or another appropriate argument to establish whether the point is a maximum or minimum.

sections.heading: Interpret the result
sections.body: State the requested dimensions or quantity with units where relevant. A mathematically valid negative length is outside the domain and must be rejected. For a bounded domain, an endpoint may give an extreme value even if its derivative is not zero. An optimisation result is only as applicable as its model assumptions, such as fixed material length or negligible thickness.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Worked search and sort traces

sections.heading: Keep state and comparison separate
sections.body: A trace records what changes as each instruction executes. For a search, keep the current position or lower and upper bounds visible. A comparison does not automatically update every variable; apply only the update specified by the algorithm. An empty search range should produce a not-found outcome rather than attempt an invalid index.

sections.heading: Compare adjacent passes and insertion steps
sections.body: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps an out-of-order pair. A left-to-right ascending pass moves a large value towards the right. Insertion sort instead maintains a sorted prefix and inserts the next value into its correct place. Record the precise state after the requested pass or insertion, because two methods can produce the same final sorted list by different intermediate steps.

sections.heading: Merge ordered parts carefully
sections.body: Merge sort divides the sequence into smaller parts and combines sorted parts by repeatedly selecting the next smallest available element. All values must be retained, including duplicates. A trace should not silently discard equal items or treat them as a single value unless the algorithm explicitly removes duplicates. Algorithm names matter less than accurately following the operations and termination conditions.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.title: Arrays, files and defensive input handling

sections.heading: Validate before converting and using
sections.body: Input arrives in a form defined by the interface, commonly a string. Check permitted form and conversion behaviour before treating it as a numerical quantity. Then check its range or other domain constraints. A valid-looking number may still be inappropriate for the task. Keep an error response distinct from successful processing, and preserve useful user input when an operation fails.

sections.heading: Handle empty and boundary cases
sections.body: An array of n items indexed from zero has valid indices 0 through n − 1. Iterating to n inclusive causes an out-of-range access. A total can be zero for valid data, so do not confuse that value with an empty collection. A mean needs a non-zero count. File handling should consider a missing file, an empty file and malformed records separately where required by the program specification.

sections.heading: Use a clear subprogram interface
sections.body: Pass needed data through parameters and return a defined result or failure representation. Avoid relying on hidden global variables when a local value is sufficient. A caller must check the success result before announcing completion. Testing should include a normal record, the smallest valid input, a missing record and a representative invalid record rather than only repeating a successful example.

topics.code_example:
FUNCTION meanOf(values)
    IF LENGTH(values) = 0 THEN
        RETURN "no data"
    ENDIF
    total ← 0
    FOR EACH value IN values
        total ← total + value
    NEXT value
    RETURN total / LENGTH(values)
ENDFUNCTION

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Choosing materials with evidence

sections.heading: Start with the failure mode
sections.body: A material decision should specify the product requirement before naming a material. A shelf needs adequate stiffness and load capacity; a transparent guard may need toughness, clarity and suitable heat resistance; an outdoor fitting may need corrosion resistance. Geometry, thickness, grain direction and support spacing influence the performance as well as the material name.

sections.heading: Compare realistic candidates
sections.body: Timber can offer appearance and workability but changes with moisture. Plywood can provide useful panel stability; MDF provides uniform machining behaviour but needs suitable dust control and a grade suited to exposure. Aluminium alloys offer low density, while steels can provide high stiffness for common structural uses. Polymers differ greatly in impact response, surface hardness, heat behaviour and processing. Select a grade, not an imagined universal material family.

sections.heading: Use evidence to justify the trade-off
sections.body: A comparison table should connect properties to the actual design. Explain why a disadvantage is acceptable or how it is addressed by construction. Consider available stock, processes, tools, finishes, cost, repair and end of life. A score without a stated basis can create false precision. Support the choice with prototype evidence or relevant material information, and revisit it if a test reveals an important failure.

topics.subject: Design & Technology
topics.title: Ergonomics, prototypes and product testing

sections.heading: Test a defined user task
sections.body: Ergonomics concerns effective and comfortable interaction, while anthropometrics supplies relevant body measurements. Identify who will use the product, in what posture, for what task and under which constraints. A handle can fail through poor clearance or reach even if its material is strong. Select dimensions for an appropriate user range rather than assuming the average measurement suits everyone.

sections.heading: Build a prototype to answer a question
sections.body: A low-cost model can investigate grip, access, arrangement or proportion. A structural sample can investigate a joint or material choice. Decide the question before building, choose a method capable of answering it, and record observations clearly. A visual model alone cannot validate a loaded structure; a destructive test is not automatically appropriate for an assessed school product. Plan safe tests with the teacher.

sections.heading: Turn results into development
sections.body: Compare evidence with measurable specification criteria and relevant user feedback. Explain the cause of a weakness before proposing a change. A wider base may improve stability but use more space; a larger handle may improve clearance but interfere with storage. Retest an appropriate modified model or sample. Evaluation should document both strengths and limitations without fabricating a perfect outcome.
